speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should correct the record right away. I am told that I used the word "exposed" rather than "imposed".
This move will ensure that unusual export demand for these products does not impair supplies to Canadian consumers.
During the debate in the House on May 28 on the subject of possible controls I stated that the government had this matter under review. I added that it was hoped that consultations with refiners would result in agreements suitable to the needs of the Canadian market. The National Energy Board has been in contact with the refiners but was unable to get universal acceptance of a willingness to limit exports of the supplies in question. Further, a significant portion of the export trade is in the hands of independent jobbers whose interest, understandably, is in the development of profitable trading opportunities and who, therefore, are less responsive to persuasion by the National Energy Board.
Because of the very substantial differences which exist between American and Canadian prices, there was no assurance that exports of these products could be voluntarily limited at this time. The government, on the advice of the National Energy Board, has therefore decided to impose export controls for a temporary period. The regulations covering this will be tabled later. At this time I also wish to announce that there will be a repeal of the import restrictions on motor gasoline. The duration of the temporary period will be related to improvement in international supplies of refined oil products and also to the expansion of refinery capacity in eastern Canada.
In concluding, I would remind the House that eastern Canada is necessarily dependent on the international petroleum economy. Imports of refined products continue to be required. Particularly in the case of heating oils, they will not be easy to obtain this year, but the government expects that Canadian oil companies will make every effort to ensure that we enter the heating season with adequate inventories.

subtopic: FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister used the right word when he said "exposed" because never have we had more explicit proof of the fact that the government is reacting all the time to the pressures put upon it. The motion debated in the House on May 28 asked for the imposition of controls and the minister said he would consider the matter. Quite frankly, I am glad he has made this move to

stop the monkeyshines that have been going on in the pricing of gasoline and heating fuels across Canada in the last few weeks. In passing, I wish I could persuade the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) to be just as helpful to house builders by putting export controls on lumber.
There are two points I would like to make. One is that our national policy in Canada has been to try to increase the processing in Canada of products made out of our basic resources, and of course oil is one. We have been running at a deficit of nine to one with the Americans on trade in processed products coming from the refineries in our two countries. Our national policy has been to try to bring that into better balance. The policy announced today puts a check on decreasing that deficit in the interests of the security of the moment. However, I hope the minister will keep in mind one paragraph in his statement, that he is watching the refinery capacity in eastern Canada very closely, because a good deal of economic impetus can be given to the well-being of the Maritimes and Quebec by the export of finished products from the big refineries on stream and coming on stream and this is very important to eastern Canada. I would hope that in the national interest this will be considered by the minister and that he will move on it a little more expeditiously than he did in deciding to make the statement he made today.
Finally, in regard to what I think is an even more important part of the minister's statement today I point out that he indicated a slight concern for the precarious situation facing the people of Montreal and eastern Canada, including Ottawa, with respect to heating fuel each winter as time goes on. We rely at the moment on offshore resources. I suggest that, instead of leaving it up to private enterprise to secure adequacy of supply for this very important part of Canada in the years to come, the minister should come off his high horse, his big deals with OECD, where he works on an academic formula in case there is a shortage and make a Canada-Venezuela deal which will guarantee our supply in case of any crisis in the Middle East. The main purpose of my response to the minister's statement is to indicate that security of supply for Montreal and the other parts of eastern Canada has not been provided.
The energy situation in the world today is a great danger to the world but, because of our possession of great resources in this field, it provides a great opportunity for Canada. I would appeal to the minister and to the people on his side of the House to make some sort of move and establish clearcut energy guidelines so that we can take advantage of this great opportunity not only for the present emergency but for many decades to come.

subtopic: FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Last January the minister was quite insistent that there was no shortage of crude oil supplies in Canada, but by February 15 he was compelled by the realities of the situation to impose export controls on crude oil. On May 28, when I moved my motion calling for three items, one of them being export controls on gasoline and other refined products, the minister felt that there was no need for any action. Now, of course, he has announced that controls will begin tomorrow night at midnight.
I do not know whether the minister is being badly advised or whether the National Energy Board is not fully aware of the situation, but almost any person in the oil industry could have told the minister any time in the last three months that we were heading into trouble. What is unfortunate is that when the government does impose export controls it sets them at the inflated figure to which exports have risen. For instance, exports of crude oil used to be around half a million barrels a day and climbed to about three-quarters of a million barrels, but when the minister refused to act last January and waited until February 15 our crude oil exports had gone up to one and a quarter million barrels, and that is roughly where the minister imposed export controls.
What I want to know, and I hope the minister will tell us in the regulations or in a statement to the House, is what the export quotas for gasoline are going to be. In the month of April our exports of gasoline had climbed to 17,850,000 gallons which was more than we had exported in all of the year 1972. If he sets the export controls at that figure, then the export controls are, of course, absolutely meaningless.

subtopic: FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that when the oil companies were prevented from exporting crude oil they decided to export gasoline which was another way of exporting oil. While the minister kept claiming that this did not involve Canadian oil, and that most of it was from offshore oil refined in eastern Canada, the hon. Mr. Grossman, Minister of Revenue in the province of Ontario, scuttled that argument by pointing out that in the month of March, Ontario, where only western Canadian crude is refined, had exported 4.1 million gallons.
I also hope that the minister will take some steps to assure supplies in those areas that are not supplied by western Canadian crude, such as in eastern Canada. In British Columbia, where they use western crude, much of it is exported to the United States and is refined and shipped back. With the present price structure in the United States that supply is being cut off, not only gasoline but also heating fuel and bunker "C" which is very important for ferries, diesel trains and diesel engines. I hope the minister is going to apply himself to that problem before winter is upon us.
In the motion I moved on May 28 I raised the question of a two-price system and I want to return to that. I hope the minister is now giving consideration to providing some

June 14, 1973
Gasoline and Home Heating Oil Export Controls protection to oil and gasoline consumers in Canada against the pressure of rising external prices. There is no reason why the oil companies who are allowed to sell oil to the United States should not get the American price, but there is absolutely no reason why they should charge that price to Canadian consumers.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Yesterday the President of the United States gave the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a lead by fixing the price of gasoline at the gasoline pumps. We may not have these wide sweeping powers in Canada but since the federal government controls the pipelines there are ways by which we can protect the Canadian consumer from the oil companies who are taking advantage of the higher prices in the United States and raising prices unnecessarily in Canada so that they can enhance their already inflated profits. The time has come for the government to move on this situation and not wait until another crisis is upon us.

subtopic: FUNDY TIDES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said just now that he had warned the government about what is now happening. Only yesterday, my colleague from Compton (Mr. Latulippe) moved a motion for the House to adjourn, under Standing Order 26, so as to study this matter of oil, gasoline and crude oil. At the time the Chair stated, and I quote:
.. . the minister appeared before the committee to discuss the production and distribution of oil products. I allude to previous discussions, not that I claim that the matter has been discussed exhaustively and that it need not be the subject of other debates, but because at this point it must be determined whether the problem entails the element of pressing and urgent necessity, due to recent events, which is normally required to justify a debate under Standing Order 26.
Mr. Speaker, 24 hours later the minister makes a statement to the effect that the matter is urgent. He now says that we must take immediate steps to control exports in our oil, gasoline and heating fuel production sectors.
The minister also said, and I quote:
In concluding, I would remind the House that eastern Canada is necessarily dependent on the international petroleum economy.
Not the Canadian industry, no, but the international economy.
Imports of refined products continue to be required. .. they will not be easy to obtain this year ...
That means that eastern Canada is in danger; we have no assurances that the countries which now supply eastern Canada with oil will be able to continue to do so.
Mr. Speaker, if I understand correctly, eastern Canada extends from Kingston to the Atlantic Ocean, and western Canada from Kingston to the Pacific Ocean; this means that part of Ontario, the entire province of Quebec and the Maritime provinces make up eastern Canada. The citizens of eastern Canada have no assurances that the exporting countries will be able to sell us the refined products we need.
The minister added and I quote:
Particularly in the case of heating fuels, they will not be easy to obtain this year, but the government expects that Canadian oil companies will make every effort. . .
He is still not sure.
... to ensure that we enter the heating season with adequate inventories.
Mr. Speaker, we are in June. Why wait two or three months to take efficient measures which would enable Western Producers-from Alberta and elsewhere in Canada-to assure supplies in Eastern Canada of gasoline and heating fuel necessary for next winter. The government always wait until it is too late to introduce measures after having repeated for months that conditions are not urgent. Now we are told right and left that the price of gasoline and heating fuel will be increased. On the other hand, Alberta producers complain because they could increase their production to supply the large Canadian market, but they are not allowed to export. Very well, however, let us take the necessary steps to import oil from Alberta and other oil-producing provinces, in order that their production be supplied to Eastern Canada so that the people in that area will benefit from the natural resources of the whole Canada, while the people in the West would benefit from some other natural resources.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
That this House no longer has confidence in the government which, by its weak and stubborn adherence to outmoded policies, increasingly burdens the people of Canada with grievous cost of living increases.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this motion which refers to the most important issue facing Canadians in all walks of life-the general management of the economy and the way in which the cost of living has been increasing. Between April and May on this year we experienced the largest increase in the cost of living in this country in any similar period in 25 years and we have seen, in the statistics, that the inflation rate has increased to about 6 per cent. No one, however, needs to look at statistics to know that the cost of living has increased by an amount which is almost unheralded in this country. Everyone who walks into a store and buys goods and services knows this fact.
The cost to Canadians of the inability of our government to deal with the problems of inflation are almost incalculable. The ravages it exerts on people on fixed incomes who see their pension wiped out because of inflation, the destruction of savings that takes place because of inflation, the erosion of confidence by people who are trying to save, the eradication of hope which takes place when young people think they never have a chance to buy

a house because of inflation-all these things make it imperative that something be done about this tremendous problem in the economy at the present time.
Certainly, the question of inflation and the kind of inflation we have today is not unrelated to the total problem of unemployment which we have had in the nation over the last couple of years. There is no question that a large increase in the cost of living and a large increase in inflation effects our position in international markets and, certainly as time goes by, if inflation continues our trade must suffer.
I want to point out very carefully to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) that we are not obsessed by inflation in this particular party as he might have suggested a few days ago when we were speaking on this matter. We are not obsessed by inflation; in fact we have always said that we are quite prepared to accept a small amount of inflation in order to have full employment in our economy if this is the price that we have to pay. I want to point out to the hon. member that it is a great deal different, however, to accept 2 per cent inflation than to have an inflationary rate of 6 per cent or 6 V2 per cent.
I want to point out also to the hon. member that while our inflation rate during the previous years has been less than that of some other countries in the world, the fact of the matter is that there are countries, such as the United States and Great Britain, where the inflation rate is being brought down while our inflation rate is going up and our comparative advantage toward those countries is declining every day. It seems to me that we cannot ignore the fact that if we do not do something about the inflation problem we may some day be faced with the problem of doing something about employment.
Most important, while we are not obsessed in this party about the problem of inflation, although we certainly could not possibly accept a 6 per cent inflation rate in the nation, we are obsessed about the fact that the economy must be fully employed, that people who need jobs can find jobs and that we use our resources effectively and efficiently. I am frightened as I witness what is happening in this country now, and the type of policy that we see enacted by the government, that the government may be in desperation going back to the policies that were followed two or three years ago when it slowed down the economy, and had high levels of unemployment to try to stop inflation.
No Canadian, no member of parliament, can in good conscience sit in this House and watch this happen. It seems to me that it is of utmost importance that we keep in mind that when we want to do something about the inflationary situation in the nation today, we are not doing that only to protect the people who are badly hurt by inflation, but we want to avoid the possibility of going back to a policy that did not work before, and I do not think would work again.
I hope this afternoon that in the course of the next few hours we will have a very serious debate about the reasons for the inflation in the economy and the reasons for the unemployment we had a couple of years ago and the policies that the government is following. Nobody in this House or in any particular party has a vested interest in trying to cure these problems. Everyone is concerned. No
June 14, 1973

one is satisfied with the inflationary rate. But we must accept that this is the federal parliament. If there is one responsibility that is put in the hands of the federal government, it is the responsibility for monetary and fiscal matters on a national basis. This is a responsibility that we cannot ignore. We cannot possibly go back to our ridings and say that we did not do anything about the inflation problem in this nation. All of us have a full responsibility for trying to cure this desperate situation. It seems to me that what we are really debating is not that something has to be done, but what should be done and how it should be done.
What is the government's answer to the inflation problem that we have in the nation today? As I understand it, the government is taking a position on four or five points. First, that basically inflation is a worldwide problem and we cannot really do very much about it on a domestic basis-that it is caused by rising world incomes that are pushing up demand in various countries around the world. Second, the government seems to be taking the position that cost-push inflation in this economy is no longer very important; that it is not as important as demand-pull inflation in Canada. Third, it is saying, it seems to me, that if anything can be done about inflation in Canada we have to do it through the operation of broad general monetary and fiscal policies; that selective controls or general controls of any sort are not necessary and certainly would not work. Fourth, that if they are going to do anything about inflation they are going to do it by operating through the supply side by trying to increase the supply of goods and services, rather than by operating on the demand side.
Let us examine these contentions and see how correct they may be. I would not argue, and no one in this party would argue, that there are no demand pressures developing around the world, that there is not inflation in other countries at the present time, but I do not think we should overrate this fact. The fact of the matter is, if you look at the statistics between 1971 and 1972 when there was worldwide inflation, it was possible for certain countries to reduce their rate of inflation. The rate of inflation between those years went down in Great Britain and in the United States as well as other European countries, but at the same time our rate of inflation went up.
There has never been a direct correlation between changes in the rate of inflation in other countries and the change in the rate of inflation in our country. It is ignoring some of the realities of our economy to suggest that there is nothing we can do about inflation in this country because it is a worldwide phenomenon. Obviously, the world situation has some effect but it is an abdication of responsibility to think that we do not have to do anything about it ourselves. The force which created inflation in Canada three years ago, two years ago, which was cost-push inflation has never been dealt with. They are still present in the economy and are still contributing to the inflation that we have now.
This party rejects totally the notion that we are not sovereign in the making of economic policies in this country, that we cannot find some method in Canada to deal with the problems of inflation and the problems of unemployment. Moreover, Canada has the responsibility of
Cost of Living
doing more than we are doing. After all, Canada was one of the nations that signed the agreement on the International Monetary Fund, trying to stop worldwide inflation. I, for one, find it a little tedious to hear the government constantly excusing its performance by trying to find some country where things are not working as well as in Canada and saying "ha, ha, we cannot to any better than X-country someplace else." It is time for Canada to face its own responsibility-not only to the people of Canada but the people of the world and to come to grips with inflationary problems. We are not helpless before the world as far as the inflationary situation is concerned.
Another point the government is making is that it is dealing with inflation by increasing the supply of goods and services. Certainly, in the long run that is the way in which the problem must be dealt with. However, as Lord Keynes used to say, "in the long run we are all dead". We must have solutions in the short run. We must be convinced whether or not the government is following consistent policies on the supply side. I will not dwell on the programs adopted two or three years ago for not growing as much wheat as we could, because wheat was in over supply, or the flock reduction program. Instead, let us look at the situation as it exists now.
One of the most inflationary factors in the economy today is the cost of housing. The rapid increase in the price of housing is exerting enormous inflationary pressure on the economy of the country. Certainly, if a person comes home and finds that his rent has been increased, he is going to demand higher wages, and properly so, if he wants to maintain his standard of living. We have an enormous housing shortage in this country and the fact that house prices are going up so fast is, in itself, evidence that there is a shortage.
What is the government doing now to try to take action against that shortage? What is happening? Regardless of what anyone on the government side may suggest, mortgage interest rates are going up, while at the same time housing starts in Canada have decreased. We know in this country, as has been evident throughout the postwar period, that when mortgage rates hit 9 l/i per cent, residential building slows down. In fact, one of the characteristic features of the Canadian economy in the postwar years has been this countercyclical activity in housing. When interest rates go up, I am speaking of mortgage interest rates, house building drops off. That is what we are seeing right now. By following a policy that is allowing mortgage interest rates to rise, not only is the government making it impossible for hundreds of thousands of Canadians ever to own a home, but the government is hindering the increase in the supply of housing. And yet increasing supply is supposed to be the heart and soul of the government's policy.
Equally important, in other areas the government is not following supply policies at all. Certainly, nothing has been said until today, and I am referring to the announcement of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), about relating our domestic production to domestic needs. Everyone knows that lumber prices have soared in this country because of the tremendous demand for lumber from foreign sources. People know that the

output of mills in the various parts of this country is completely sold out to foreigners, and this is forcing up the price in the domestic market. And yet we have heard nothing about a coherent program on the part of the government to look after the domestic supply needs of Canadian consumers.
As far as monetary policy is concerned, interest rates have been rising and continue to rise. What happens in the monetary system when this occurs? First, the large customers by and large are accommodated. The higher interest rates do not affect them, because they are able to pass them on in the form of higher prices. Actually, if one were to draw any correlation between interest rates and rates of investment in the recent past, one would see that high interest rates have not slowed down the investment of large corporations.
But what about the small borrower-the farmer, the small businessman, the fisherman or the homeowner? They are the first people to be affected. They are the people who cannot get loans. They are the people whose activity is stopped. Yet, they are the ones who ought to be involved in increasing output in our economy. The government now says that it is attempting to monitor whether or not these people are getting loans. It need not monitor very much. Every day I am sure members of this House are getting calls from constituents who find that they are unable to get loans and funds at a rate which they formerly paid. In its supply policies, one would have thought that the government would have removed the sales tax on building materials, but it did not do so. One would have thought that in the budget it would have tried to stimulate output from small businesses, but this was not done. So, if the government is saying, "We are going to cope with inflation in Canada by increasing supply", I say that there is absolutely no evidence of any consistent program for attacking supply in a coherent fashion.
Where the government can most be faulted is in the area of general monetary and fiscal policy, in its broad-gauge use of monetary and fiscal policy to govern the operation of the economy for a number of years. The government has taken the position that it is possible to essentially fine tune the economy and bring about price stability, full employment and growth by using monetary and fiscal measures alone. This is just not so. It may have been true 25 years ago, or 30 years ago, but it certainly is not true today.
The reasons for this, it seems to me, are fourfold. In the first place, monetary and fiscal policies as we know them are designed to work in perfectly competitive economies. The Canadian economy is not perfectly competitive. That was made very clear in the early 1970's, when the government followed a policy of restricting output. Prices did not fall. We had the strange situation of having an unemployment level of 7.1 per cent, and the only thing that happened was that there was a decline in output. There was no decline in prices. Actually, prices continued to rise. If monetary and fiscal policies were to operate as they should in theory, obviously, during that period of time prices would have fallen. But they did not. All that happened was that economic activity was restricted, and prices continued to rise. It is clear that we were operating

then in a period of cost-push inflation and that monetary policies simply were not effective.
Second, the government seems to think that it can use monetary and fiscal policies alone to achieve price stability and full employment, because it thinks it can estimate what will be the impact of the changes that monetary and fiscal policies will bring to the economy over a period of time. However, we do not know what those effects will be. The one piece of evidence which seems to be clear is that, we do not have sufficient information to know when the effects of changes in these policies are really going to take place. I remind the minister that as recently as last year he thought, from the evidence available to him, that the government was operating with a budgetary deficit. It turned out, however, that there was a surplus. Indeed, the whole policy thrust was different from what was contemplated because of the lack of information from which he suffered at that particular time. Because of this lack of information and predictability of when monetary and fiscal policies are going to work, broad and blunt instruments alone are not adequate to deal with the economy.
The third reason that monetary and fiscal policies will not work as effectively as hoped in the economy is that the Canadian economy is structurally different from that of almost any other country in the world. We are different because of the large degree of foreign ownership in our economy. Manufacturing is probably 57 per cent foreign owned; the mining industries are probably 55 per cent foreign owned; oil, gas and coal mines are about 82 per cent foreign owned; petroleum refining is about 99 per cent foreign owned, and so on. I am not speaking about this from the standpoint of whether it is good or bad, but from the standpoint of what effect this has on the operation of our economy. Usually, under normal fiscal policies, if there is a cut in taxes, especially in corporate taxes, you would expect an increase in investment. However, if in the economy, decisions about increases in investment are made somewhere else, then, whether or not that effect will take place is a question that is not certain. There may not be that response at all.
The same may be said with respect to monetary policy. In a situation where your capital markets and banking system are intertwined with those of another country then, although you may change your monetary policy, the effects may not be those that you expected. There is a suggestion that when the bank rate was first increased in Canada, it was increased in response to heavy borrowings on the part of foreign corporations, basically corporations domiciled in the United States. As the short-term rate in Canada was lower than the short-term rate in the United States, they came here to borrow. Because of the great intermixing of our two capital markets, the only response that the government could think of was to increase the discount rate. That sent all our interest rates up, causing all of us to pay more. The government did that because of its adherence to the proposition that you must not interfere with the broad operation of monetary and fiscal methods.
Clearly, it makes absolutely no sense to see all interest rates in Canada go up, particularly at the long end of the market, to see mortgage rates and consumer loan rates rise, simply because foreign corporations are borrowing
June 14, 1973

heavily from the Canadian banking system because our short-term rates are lower than those in other countries. One would have thought that in this situation we would have heard some serious debate about the possibilities of a domestic interest equalization tax or something of that nature. The fact is that broad-gauge monetary and fiscal policies, as used in Canada over the past 15 to 25 years simply cannot be counted on to give price stability, reasonable growth and reasonably full employment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue before the House, the motion raised by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) is, of course, one of concern to the Canadian people and of deep concern to the government. The inflationary pressures which confront us at the moment concern us because of their effect in eroding the incomes of Canadian families, reducing the value of savings and undermining Canada's competitive position in world markets. I do not want to underestimate the hurt caused to Canadian families by this economic phenomenon.
I want to say, though-and I think the House is entitled to review the facts-that despite the adverse impact of inflation there continues to be an increase in the real income of Canadians. In the first quarter of this year the real disposable income of Canadians per capita, that is after payment of direct taxation and after making allowance for the higher cost of living, was up 4.9 per cent as compared with the level a year ago.
I think the House is entitled to look at the comparison of incomes and prices and to review the facts which are published quarterly by Statistics Canada. Incomes in this country are still, fortunately, outstripping prices. As a government, we have long wrestled with this problem of inflationary pressures. I want to suggest to the hon. member for Don Valley that it does not lend itself to easy or slick solutions. We have been and remain prepared in the government to adopt any policies which would effectively moderate the upward movement of prices and which would, on balance, over a reasonable time, benefit the Canadian people and the economy. The policies we are using at the moment are, first, to increase the supply of those commodities whose production has fallen short of growing demand, thus contributing to rising cost. We are encouraging food production. In the area of housing we are trying to inject more funds into the market-trying to stabilize the price of land by promoting less costly land assembly. So, we are increasing supply on one hand and increasing the disposable income of Canadians on the other.
As to the latter proposition, I should like to review the budgetary policy of the government for a few moments. I refer to the measure to reduce income tax progressively, in favour of lower income groups, by 12 to 13 per cent under a $100 float and a $500 ceiling, the elimination of federal sales tax on all items of food and drink, excepting alcohol; the elimination of federal sales tax on all items of children's clothing and shoes; reduction of the tariffs on agricultural and manufactured products having a consumer appeal, to the extent of $1,400,000,000; raising the old age pension to $100 a month; raising the guaranteed income supplement, and raising the supplement for both married and single persons; proposing, as we did, through my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), an increase in the family allowance to $20 per month per child-

But there are distinct differences between the policies of the government at the moment and the policies of the government in 1969-70. To begin with, the bank rate, at 614 per cent, is at least one and a half or two points below what it was in those years. The money supply is still expanding at about 20 per cent and bank loans were expanding in the first five months of 1973 at an annual rate of 30 per cent. In those years, between 1969 and 1970, the increase in bank loans was held at 2 per cent. So, there is no foundation for the argument that the policy of the government today parallels the policy pursued in 1969-70. Indeed, the underlying circumstances are different.
In 1968-69 there had been a period of prolonged expansion in this country. At the moment, there is still a gap between the actual and the potential of the economy and unemployment is still too high. In 1969-70, there was a pronounced wage escalation. Wage rates rose at a rate of about 7.5 per cent in the first quarter of 1973, which is below the rate of 7.8 per cent in 1972. There has not been any break-out in wages. In 1969-70, the international position was far different from what it is now. Europe was in a period of recession whereas at the present time every industrial economy of the world is expanding strongly. This expansion is producing contageous results; it is promoting some of the increased world demand for commodities, particularly food, the prime cause of inflation here.
Then again, in 1969-70 we had a fixed exchange rate. Now, we have a floating exchange rate. So, the argument attempting to equate the policy of the government today with the policy which might have been in effect in 1969-70 does not happen to be well founded. The government long ago drew up comprehensive contingency plans for the establishment of price and income controls and we remain ready to implement those plans if, as and when we become convinced they can play a sufficiently effective role in moderating inflationary pressures, so to justify such drastic intervention by the state in the economic affairs of every Canadian citizen.
June 14, 1973

As I have emphasized many times in the House, however, we have not adopted such controls and are not prepared to adopt them under circumstances prevailing today because we do not believe they would make any significant contribution to alleviating the particular problem which is confronting us. Indeed, if we tried to make such control effective, we could very well cause considerably more harm than good to the Canadian people by reducing the supply of goods and as a result only aggravate inflationary pressures. Undoubtedly some of the inflationary forces in this country originate domestically. That is undoubtedly so. The underlying cost push pressures which have plagued all industrial nations in recent years have been aggravated, however, by a tremendous demand for goods and services resulting from strong growth in the Canadian economy. By far the greater inflationary pressures confronting us in Canada today are worldwide in their origin. The major upward thrust here and abroad has come from a sharp rise in food prices.
Increases in food prices are due basically to the fact that global supplies of food commodities were sharply reduced by adverse weather conditions around the world at a time when the demand for food, particularly the demand for meat, was rising sharply in response to the substantially increasing economies of every industrial nation. This is particularly and markedly true in the case of Japan which has turned into a consumer-oriented country, now entering the worldwide consumer markets for meat, sugar, clothing and even for French wine. Japan is using some of its huge reserves to get into consumer markets, and this affects world commodity prices everywhere.
The increase in food prices is compounded by soaring costs of a wide variety of international trading commodities including soyabeans and fertilizer which incidentally, are some of the ingredients that go into the cost of farming. As of March, prices of such global commodities, that is world trading commodities, were up 53 per cent over the level of a year ago. Some commodities rose considerably more than that. At the beginning of the year cattle hides were up 126 per cent over the 12 month level a year ago and wool 83 per cent. There are many others, and these are the commodities that are being boosted in price because of an imbalance between supply and demand. There is nothing any domestically oriented controlled system will be able to do about that type of situation.

I listen to the hon. member for Don Valley with interest everytime he speaks. I have listened to him suggest how we are going to make this country less vulnerable to world economic trends, yet here we are, a major international trading nation, with about 25 per cent of our gross national product depending on foreign trade.
For many years we in Canada have benefited substantially from a massive flow of goods and capital regularly across our borders. While there are circumstances in which Canada can take practical steps to moderate the adverse impact of developments abroad, it is unrealistic to expect that we can totally insulate ourselves from these
Cost of Living
forces and still expect to gain the considerable advantages that accrue to us as a major trading nation. We just cannot do it.
The hon. gentleman has asked whether we might do something in respect of a domestic equalization tax. Even if we did that, what might the consequences be? Would the United States eliminate its exemptions which accrue to us from the United States equalization tax? If that happened, would it not in fact have an adverse effect on our interest rates by depriving Canadians access to United States capital markets? I suggest to the hon. member that if he thinks this through he might realize it could well have a contrary effect to the one he has suggested. I will refer to that matter perhaps at the end of my speech.

Yes, but it would not benignly effect the interest rates, as the hon. gentleman suggests, and that was the context of the argument of the hon. member for Don Valley when he made that point.
In summary what I am trying to say, worldwide inflationary trends affect Canada as they do every country in the world. This is essentially a demand situation involving an imbalance in supply and demand of agricultural products and of world products. It is not primarily at this stage a cost-push situation. As I have said before, wages have not broken out, profits are recovering from the depressed position during 1970-71 and the price of durables has remained remarkably constant in historic terms.
Let me turn my attention more directly to the terms of the motion before the House, which condemns the government for its alleged responsibility for the increase in cost of living of Canadians because of its, and I use the words of the motion, "weak and stubborn adherence to outmoded policies". I think parenthetically I am entitled to point out that the motion itself is a contradiction of terms, since it is not evident how the government could adhere weakly and stubbornly at the same time to any given policy, good, bad or indifferent. Either we are weak or we are strong and stubborn, but we cannot be both at the same time.

-anyone who thinks that inflation in the nation today is coming from excess demand in the economy certainly is misinterpreting the inflationary situation in totality.

Only a few months later, however, the member radically changed his diagnosis of the problem. Speaking in the debate which he also originated on May 10, like this one, he declared, and this is to be found at page 3616 of Hansard:
I accept the explanation given by the Minister of Finance that there have been great difficulties throughout the world in terms of food supplies, rising incomes and the rising expectations of people who are using more food. I accept those statements and would not debate them here today.
Those are his words, and small wonder he chose not to debate them. He says the situation is the result of a cost-push factor, and then he takes the other position. I ask who was inexcusably misinterpreting the inflationary situation in totality? That contradiction is no isolated case.

speechtext:
May I pose a question to the minister? Could there not be a matter of cost-push in demand and inflation at the same time? Moreover, does the minister

not suggest that the situation in respect of the Canadian economy has been evolving and changing over the period of the last six months?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have always understood the hon. member he has been suggesting that wage and price controls are a Galbraithian formula to counteract the cost-push. Now, he is finally admitting-and I have tried to cite examples from three speeches-that there is basically a demand-pull situation which in world commodities and agricultural commodities is not subject to that Gabraithian formula.
Now, let us move on to another area of economic policy. We have a full debate in terms of the motion before us, Mr. Speaker. Let us look at the exchange rate. In the budget debate the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), as recorded at page 1559 of Hansard, questioned the value of the floating Canadian exchange rate and asserted that Canada has never enjoyed really high levels of prosperity since the Canadian dollar appreciated in relation to United States currency. But in the House of Commons on June 5, 1973, another hon. member of the Conservative financial troika, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), derided the government for an alleged decision "to ride along with the U.S. dollar". While no such decision was ever made by the government, the clear implication of his question was that the government in some way should take action to increase the value of the Canadian dollar in relation to overseas currencies and in relation to the United States dollar. I wonder what the member for Don Valley thinks that would do for Canadian prosperity? I suggest when they have a free moment they try to work that one out.
I should now like to turn to the question of the monetary policy elucidated by the front bench of the opposition. In recent weeks, the hon. member for Don Valley has attempted to represent the move by the Bank of Canada to moderate the exceptionally rapid increase of credit in Canada as a return to tight money policies aimed at drastically restricting economic growth. I suggest that these statements approach the hypocritical. I want to point out that as long ago as January 26 of this year, as recorded at page 679 of Hansard, the same hon. member asked whether in view of the recent increase in wholesale prices I had discussed changing the money supply with the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I can only presume that by changing the money supply he was urging me to press for its reduction in light of his previous warning in his newspaper column-and I refer again to the hon. member's column on the subject of monetary policy in the Toronto Telegram of September 27, 1971-that excessive increases in the money supply were the primary cause of the inflation.
Here are the words which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of September 27, 1971:
The proper method of lowering unemployment and slowing inflation in Canada is to bring the money supply under control and increase consumer demand substantially by cutting personal taxes .. .
June 14, 1973

That is what the hon. member told us when he wrote in his capacity as a professional economist before he entered the field of the changing winds of political participation.
Let me go on to the question of fiscal policy and economic growth because these conflicts and contradictions are as nothing when compared with the Conservative stand on the basic issue of government economic policy. I think the hon. member for Don Valley posed the issue himself, which was supported by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and by the hon. member for Edmonton West, when he told the House during the budget debate last February 22, as recorded at page 1559 of Hansard, this:
The really fundamental question one has to ask in considering this budget and its effect on employment in the economy is: is the deficit large enough to really move this country ahead, to produce the sort of employment that Canadians have every reason to expect and to hope for within the economy?
You will recall, Your Honour, that the member's answer to that rhetorical question was a resounding no. He said a Conservative government would have run a deficit two and a half times that projected in the budget. Another member, the hon. member for Edmonton West said the party would have run up a cash requirement of $4 billion, as he attempted to lift up the estimates and throw them across the aisle of the House. There was, the hon. member for Don Valley said, no reason to believe the economy would grow strongly; the prospects for increases in exports, capital investment and inventory build-ups were all weak, while little or no stimulus would be provided for increased consumer spending.
I want to draw your attention, Your Honour, to the declaration by the same member that if a Conservative government had had an opportunity to introduce the substantially more expansionary budget which he proposed, "within one year and a half our unemployment rate would be down towards 5 per cent". That is found at page 1560 of Hansard. Let us consider the position taken by the Conservative Party against the state of the economy as it exists today. Let us consider the position of the Conservative Party, taken against that budget two or three months ago, of underestimating the expansion of the economy and calling for two and a half times the deficit we now have, and yet they come into this House saying that inflation is the problem. I wonder how much the problem might have been magnified if the deficit suggested by the hon. gentleman and his party had been accepted?

Consider that suggestion against the state of the economy as it exists today: National output has been increasing at one of the fastest paces in Canadian history, with real gross national product expanding at a seasonally-adjusted rate of 11.6 per cent in the six-month period from the fourth quarter of last year to the first quarter of this year. Exports in the first four months of 1973 were up 26.6 per cent over the same period a year ago. Business capital investment spending during the first quarter rose by 7 per cent, a larger gain than any previous period since the fourth quarter of 1965. The build-up of business inventories was $1 billion greater in the first three months of this year than in the last three months of 1972. The increase in
Cost of Living
consumer spending of 4.3 per cent in the first quarter was the largest recorded in 21 years.
What about unemployment? The hon. member for Don Valley indicated to this House that under Conservative policies it would be down toward 5 per cent by around August, 1974. I am sure all members, particularly the hon. member for Don Valley, welcomed the report by Statistics Canada only a few days ago that unemployment on a seasonally-adjusted basis was down toward 5 per cent by May of this year, 5.2 per cent to be exact.

speechtext:
That is still too high, but I believe the House will recognize that there is room for some satisfaction that the trend has been sharply downward now for several months.
What are the consequences of Conservative policy as outlined to the House of Commons and thereby through the House to the people of Canada? In a question to me in the House a few days ago, on June 12, as recorded at page 4662 of Hansard, the hon. member for Don Valley referred to the length of the lag-talking about the time lag between implementation of economic policy and the effect or thrust of that policy on the economy. The fact of the matter is that the Conservative Party grossly misjudged the strong upsurge already underway in the economy and, as a consequence of having done so, urged upon the Canadian people and the government the adoption of policies that were more than just out-moded to the time and circumstances. What he urged were policies that were a prescription for disaster at that time, in view of the expansion. That deficit of $4 billion or $5 billion recommended by the hon. member for Don Valley is not even politically oriented economics but is cosmetic economics.
A few months ago the hon. member for Don Valley was telling us that to be concerned about the danger of excess demand developing was "misinterpreting the inflationary situation in totality". In May he indicated that he may have been wrong, that there were demand forces that were already causing inflationary pressures. During the budget debate he proposed on behalf of his party to compound those demand forces by massively increasing government fiscal stimulus and spending. Contrast that position, Mr. Speaker, with that taken by the hon. member for Don Valley on June 6, when he asked whether the government was considering introducing selective credit controls to eliminate some of this excessive purchasing power in the economy. If it is excessive now, how much more excessive would it have been if by any unfortunate chance the country had given the hon. member an opportunity to put his prescriptions into practice.

Let us examine the position of the Conservative front bench on controls. Like most of the other policy prescriptions advocated by the Conservative Party, their proposal for wage and price controls is based on a totally erroneous diagnosis of the problem the controls are meant to solve. At the time he first advocated them in the name of this party, the hon. member for Don Valley was telling us that inflation was solely a cost-push problem. He has since come to acknowl-

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living
edge that the particularly acute problem facing us today is far more complex than that, that an important element behind these inflationary forces is the worldwide upsurge in demand, matched by a comparable upsurge here in Canada and a worldwide shortage of a number of foodstuffs and other basic commodities. He has, I submit to the House, basically misread the situation. The fact of the matter is that wage and price controls would do very little effectively to reduce the main sources of inflationary pressures-the rising prices of food and other international commodities.
By far the greatest proportion of the increase in food prices over the past several months has taken place at the farm gate. I am not objecting to a fair return to farmers- that return is overdue and it is about time the farmers got their fair share of the returns-but those prices happen to be a result of the farmer getting more of his fair share of the economy. I believe, as the Special Committee on Food Prices of this House is ascertaining, that it is not the result of some sudden, massive rip-off being undertaken by processors, distributors or retailers in the food chains.

speechtext:
I want to thank my friends opposite for their rapt attention.
The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham announced that their party would freeze all food prices except those at the farm gate for a period of 90 days. Yet, in the debate on May 10, the hon. member for Don Valley admitted that the freeze on all other food prices along the distribution chain would amount to an effective freeze of prices at the farm gate as well. What then are we to make of all the many reasons advanced by the member for

Northumberland-Durham for exempting farm prices from any freeze, including the fact that we are operating in a "continental or even international market" for such things as "beef on the hoof," and that fresh foods are "subject to many uncontrollable factors such as weather conditions, seasonal fluctuations and world demand." I agree with that, but he should turn to his colleague, the hon. member for Don Valley, and try to work it out with him.
The controls advocated by the Conservatives clearly would do nothing to deal with the second major source of inflationary pressures stemming from the worldwide commodity price increases. If they are not prepared to pay the market price, Canadians will not obtain these essential supplies which they must import, and if they do not obtain those supplies, prices would escalate domestically even more. By the same token, it is obvious that we cannot control the prices of a vast range of other goods imported into Canada, including a substantial proportion of the food we consume.
It is not surprising that the Conservative party should seek to bolster their own sagging position by pointing to the new, tighter phase 4 control program in the United States announced by President Nixon last night as some sort of justification for their own scheme. That was certainly the substance of the first question of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in the question period today, and it was certainly implicit in a lot of what the hon. gentleman was saying. Of course, I will want to study all aspects of the program which the president announced, but I am not persuaded that a price and income control program, regardless of the details of its administration, can be effective over any extended period of time in significantly moderating inflationary pressures under the circumstances prevailing today, namely the worldwide demand in agricultural and non-agricultural commodities.
Over the whole of the 20 month period from the time the administration first imposed a total wage and price freeze in August, 1971 to April, 1973 when a number of controls had been shifted to a new phase 3 program, consumer prices rose at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.2 per cent in the U.S., compared to an increase of 5.6 per cent in Canada. If you consider Canada's very much greater exposure to world inflationary forces because of the relatively much greater volume of trade undertaken by Canada in relation to the size of its economy, I do not consider that comparison to be unfavourable. But I want to point out to the Leader of the Opposition that since the U.S. moved to its phase 3 program, consumer prices in the three months from February to April rose at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 9 per cent in the United States, compared to 6.2 per cent in Canada. Food prices in the U.S. rose at a 25.4 per cent annual rate, despite the fact that they remained under the more rigorous phase 2 controls, compared to 15.9 per cent in Canada.
While the Conservatives may choose to find some moral support for their policies in the program announced by President Nixon last night, let me draw the attention of the House to some essential differences. Unlike the Conservatives, the president does not intend to freeze wages, nor does he intend to freeze interest or dividends or rents. Unlike the Conservatives, the president said that he did not intend to freeze the price of unprocessed agricultural
June 14, 1973

products at the farm level-the main source of inflationary pressures-because this would reduce supplies instead of increasing them and would eventually result in even higher prices for the foods Americans buy at the store. Unlike the hon. member for Don Valley, who has urged that controls become a permanent part of our fiscal mechanism-and he certainly indicated that today-the president warned that permanent controls would put the economy in a straitjacket.
There are a number of important questions raised by the program announced by the president. What, for example, will be the effect of an attempt to freeze the prices of internationally traded commodities such as lumber, copper, coffee, oil sugar and so on? Will it result in a decline in the supplies of such commodities available for import? I would be particularly interested to know whether the Conservative party believes that we in Canada should be guided by the president's proposal to impose controls on the export of food products as a means of holding down prices here at home. I wonder how such a policy would be received by the farmers of this country and what effect it would have on our balance of payments with other countries? As a matter of fact, we are studying the effect of the seeking of authorization by the president for export controls and what the reaction may be in terms of the potential of retaliation around the globe.
You will gather from all that I have said that I am not particularly concerned about being accused, nor is the government, by the hon. member for Don Valley and his party of adhering to outmoded policies because it should be clear by now that the Conservative party is bankrupt of any policies, whether moded or outmoded.

What it offers in place of policies that would provide real and lasting benefits for the Canadian people is a never ending, constantly changing, stream of nostrums and panaceas dictated by nothing more-to recall the words of the hon. member for Don Valley-than the day to day changes in events and popular moods that affect economists as anyone else. Over a period of many months we have been pursuing concerted, cohesive and consistent policies aimed at promoting strong, stable and continuing growth of production, of employment, and of the real incomes of Canadians. Of course, we continue to face a variety of problems, as we always have in the past, and the problem of cost of living currently is one of our foremost concerns and one that is troublesome and hurtful to every Canadian.
While the opposition is free to continue to offer nostrums and panaceas that hold out the promise of magical solutions to every problem, they are in the game of practising cosmetic economics. We, on the other hand, have the responsibility to do everything within our power to pursue practical, workable and effective policies that will be to the long term benefit, not the detriment, of the Canadian people. We intend to continue fulfilling that responsibility as best we can.

Mr. Speaker, it has been an entertaining half hour listening to the minister throw a Phillips Curve past the hon. member for Don Valley and his colleagues. But one assumes the minister was acting on the old principle that the best defence is offence. I think it is worth pointing out that there are many areas where the government is deeply vulnerable to criticism for its management of the economy, and particularly its approach to the problem of rising living costs, areas in which the government can act, and ought to act right now.
For example, I suggest that instead of attacking the all too vulnerable policies of the Conservatives, the minister and his colleagues might better be advised to introduce legislation which would enable the government to implement recommendations of the Food Prices Review Board, which it has set up, within a specified period of time, and permitting the government such measures as selective roll backs of prices, or prohibition of proposed increases on a selective basis. On more than one occasion the government has taken credit for the establishment of this board. Spea.ting to the Canadian Consumers Association yesterday, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) made much of the potential of the board. But the minister knows, and we know, that unless the government is prepared to follow up the recommendations of that board with some concrete action, it will not prove to have made a very substantial contribution to the problem, with which it has been set up to deal.
I was pleased to note the announcement today by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) that export controls have been established over gasoline and home heating oil. This is one method by which some influence may be exerted over the domestic cost of these products. It is a measure which I believe to have been overdue, but at least it indicates that the government is prepared to accept some of the suggestions made from this side of the House.
If it is interested in breaking the psychological factor of inflation, the government might accomplish far more by stepping in and forcing a roll back of the price increases on the 1973 GM models which have just been announced, thus indicating to corporate enterprises in this country that they must live up to undertakings given to the government, and presumably accepted in good faith by the government. I suggest that that kind of measure can have far more influence on the psychological aspect of inflation than the rather more cumbersome device alluded to, but not in great detail, by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies).
One of the most constructive steps the government could take to deal with the cost of living would be to assign a maximum interest rate to residential mortgages, to interest rates for loans to small businesses, and to consumer loans. We in this party suggested, and indeed endeavoured to have the recent bill passed through this House amended to this end, that there should be a limit on residential mortgage interest rates, and very shortly we will be dealing with a very feeble proposal of the government to provide more residential mortgage funds. But the problem is not the availability of mortgage funds; it is the

Cost of Living
availability of mortgage funds at an interest rate which puts housing within the reach of ordinary people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
The government might well consider limiting in absolute terms, or licensing, foreign borrowing in this country. The government might wel'l consider taking some general steps to lower the freight rate structure which is so central to the economy of western Canada, northern Ontario and other regions of the country, and which makes such a substantial contribution to the over-all cost of living. The government can, and I trust it will, decide that no further increase in the rates of Bell Canada is necessary. Not that that in itself will adequately deal with the cost of living, but it will telegraph to corporate enterprise in Canada, and to the people of Canada, that the government is serious about keeping a check on rising living costs.
It is not enough for the government to content itself with attacking the policies of other parties. The problem confronting this parliament, as the hon. member for Don Valley has said, is a difficult one, not susceptible to easy or simplistic solutions. But that is no excuse for the federal government merely to drift, or to react in response to crises which might well have been anticipated and acted upon earlier.
In dealing with the resolution before the House, one must look at the alternatives that have been placed forward. I listened with considerable interest to the speech of the hon. member for Don Valley because I was anxious to see to what extent today we would receive more details about this Conservative proposal for wages and prices control. First of all, he talked about a 90 day freeze. Of course, that in itself is not a new aspect of their policies, nor is it in itself a policy. It is merely a temporary delay which would be followed up by some kind of constructive action. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, a freeze in itself simply temporarily holds the situation where it is when the freeze is imposed, and when it is lifted the withholding and the holding back are ended. A surge forward takes place, and I suspect the record will show that the price levels that exist shortly after a freeze has ended are probably higher than if the freeze itself had not been imposed. A freeze is no policy at all. Therefore, one cannot accept it unless one knows what will follow the freeze. That is why I listened with such interest to the hon. member's speech today.
The hon. member for Don Valley referred to a prices and incomes board, the purpose of which would be to maintain price increases and wages increases in relation to indices of productivity and cost. I take it that this is a slight fleshing out of the wage stabilization policies which, in an earlier speech, he indicated would follow the 90 day freeze, and which he suggested would be worked out in consultation with the provinces. I take it for granted, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Don Valley is bringing into his proposal some consultation with the provinces. As I listened to him, I wondered had he any indication in advance that there would be substantial provincial co-operation with his proposal. I wondered had he fully taken into account the very substantial constitutional obstacles which stand in the way of such a proposal.

As I understand the constitution, the federal government, unless in a state of declared emergency, does not have the power to establish the kind of prices and wage controls that the hon. member is talking about. I really wonder if he is prepared, under present circumstances, to give any federal government, including one that might be composed of members of his party, the extraordinary powers to interfere in the operations of the Canadian economy that are envisaged under the peace, order and good government section of the BNA Act. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the hon. member for Don Valley I wondered what confidence he had that controls would really work. I think this is a central problem in assessing this whole inflation situation. What guarantees, what undertakings have we that controls will work?
I decided to do a little research on this problem. I turned to a document entitled "Report of the Standing Senate Committee on National Finance on Growth, Employment, and Price Stability." It struck me as being an authoritative source to which to turn for information. I refer to a chapter entitled "Guidelines, Controls and Other Policies." I read the following recommendation, which in fact was the first one made, presumably because it was the most important one:
-We are in general deeply sceptical about most varieties of controls, guidelines and incomes policies. Their historical record of effectiveness against inflation is poor, and they pose important threats to personal freedom and economic dynamism. They also tend to divert attention from more effective anti-inflationary policies. Problems of public acceptability alone would militate against selective wage/price controls. The control system would likely be either general in its application or a largely meaningless gesture. Controls are one of the least desirable of all economic stabiliziation tools. If they are used at all in peacetime it should be on a short term emergency basis.
