speechtext:
I am not one, Mr. Speaker, to attribute motives to the man who wrote those words and who today in the House has very substantially altered his position. I was curious, however, when he chided the minister and the government for not having adopted in 1971 the policy he has now put forward, because this document, authored in part by the hon. member for Don Valley, appeared in late 1971.
Whether the upward pressures on prices in Canada are caused by cost-push or demand-pull, or profit-push for that matter, seems to me to be something which we could argue all night. I suspect that one's bias depends on whether one is in or out of government. It seems to me clear that there are both cost-push and demand-pull factors operating together. One can describe certain facets of the economy where cost-push appears more prominent and one can describe other sectors where demand-pull is more
June 14, 1973

prominent; for example, energy, lumber or food. I say, therefore, that a set of economic formulae designed on the assumption that one or other alone of those causes was the root cause, would not be very intelligent.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the allusion to the operation of wage and price controls in the United States did not fill me with any particular confidence. The President of the United States announced last night that a 60-day freeze would be imposed because of what he termed run-away inflation in the United States. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the wage and price control policies of the American government have been in operation some two or three years now, and it strikes me as strange and unsubstantial proof of their success that at this point the United States government is imposing sudden freezes in order to cope with run-away inflation. I would suggest to the House that the announcement by the President of the United States last night means that controls phases I, II and III in America are not working rather than that they are working.
Too often in Canada and elsewhere, low inflation has been purchased at the cost of rising unemployment. I do not need to remind anyone in this House that that particular policy was the policy of the Liberal government in the early years of the present administration. I do not say they followed it out of bad faith, but it proved to me that ill-considered and hasty ventures into anti-inflationary policy end up hurting people who are least able to defend themselves in the marketplace and do not solve the problem. Right now in our economy the phenomenon is that we have unacceptably high levels of unemployment and unacceptably high levels of prices. I do not feel confident, on behalf of my party, that a system of controls over wages, profits, prices and incomes, so scantily detailed as the one suggested by the hon. member for Don Valley, could arrive at any solution to this difficulty.
I do not really see how he can expect the Canadian people to accept the kind of proposals he is putting forward in the absence of any details whatever as to how this board would operate, how the wage stabilization policies would operate, for how long and so on. It may well be that the simplistic and dramatic notion of freezing something appeals to people who are yearning for solutions to the difficulty, but I suggest it is dangerously misleading to suggest that the kind of proposition which is inherent in wage and price controls is going to deal with the situation at the present time. People want action, that is true, but they want action that will work and not hurt them. I think we should never lose sight of that factor.
Mr. Speaker, there is some real work facing this House of Commons. Parliament has still much important work to do. Next week legislation to raise veterans pensions will be brought into the House. We have had a solemn undertaking that the family allowances bill will be introduced and dealt with in full before the House recesses for the summer. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday indicated that an election expenses bill will be introduced in a few days. A bill dealing with takeovers and foreign investment in Canada is currently before committee. The development of a policy for western Canada built around meetings of first ministers and concentrating on economic development and including some rational approach to the
Cost of Living
reduction of freight rates ought to be a high priority for this parliament. The reorganization and decentralization of DREE is under way. We will shortly be faced with legislation affecting immigration and the immigration appeal board. There is still a lot of work in front of us in parliament, and it seems to me that when one confronts the motion we are debating this afternoon the ultimate question is quite simple: whether, taking everything into consideration, it would be in the interests of the Canadian people for parliament to dissolve at ten o'clock tonight. I make no apologies for saying that from our party the answer is no, it would not.
We shall not, therefore, support the motion presented by the hon. member for Don Valley for that reason and for the ones I have already indicated which deal with its intrinsic lacks of merit. As for rising living costs, Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much that they would be helped by an election campaign. After six months of delay, we might very well find ourselves back here with a parliamentary situation largely unchanged from what it is today. Would we not look foolish then, having spent six or seven months running around the country arguing about cost-push and demand-pull to an increasingly confused and irritated electorate, only to arrive back in mid-winter to start the whole dreary process again? I suggest there is plenty of room on the agenda for immediate action by this government, both to deal with the problem of rising living costs and to complete the agenda of the first session of this parliament. I suggest that both we and the Canadian people would be better off to get on with the job.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEAL WITH INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating the following motion:
That this House no longer has confidence in the government which, by its weak and stubborn adherence to outmoded policies, increasingly burdens the people of Canada with grievous cost of living increases.
Mr. Speaker, because I feel that this motion brought in by the Progressive Conservatives is a nonentity which includes nothing positive, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the motion be modified by replacing the final period with a comma and adding immediately after the following words:
"and because it has not given consideration to financial reforms which would have made it possible to fight against price increases and inflation by enforcing the following economic principles:
The compensated discount and the issue of new credits by the Bank of Canada to finance all new projects".
The Speaker, we have today an opportunity to highlight certain figures related to this government's administration. When we are talking about "grievous cost of living increases" we should not forget that taxes of all kinds are "public enemy No. 1."
History tells us that when a nation levies taxes in excess of 25 per cent of the income of its people, it is involved in a self-destructing process and heading for economic decadence. Currently our sales taxes eat up over one third of each earned dollar; this money is taken away painlessly from our pay cheque before we can use it. But the major
4770

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living
portion of all thoses taxes, the most beneficial for the government, is under the surface, that is to say hidden.
For instance, the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials added to the 8 per cent Quebec sales tax is a 20 per cent income for both governments while the wholesale dealer only applies a 3 to 4 per cent commission and that, on certain items, the retail dealer will content himself with a 5 to 6 per cent profit.
For the dealers who have had to truck and finance the products, we find the addition of two profits, namely 10 per cent, while the government, which did not make any effort, gets 20 per cent.
In addition to taxes not included in the sales taxes, the dealer must participate in the contributions paid by his employees to social security and unemployment insurance. He has a power bill to pay for each month; he must also pay for his truck on the roads and also 20 cents in tax on each gallon of gas used by his truck.
That merchant also pays municipal and school taxes, and all merchants and industrialists are caught in those toils.
In the automobile sector, Mr. Speaker, it is the same thing; one finds the same problem concerning the manufacturer and even the buyer. Everyone knows that when you buy an automobile, the excise tax and the sales tax combined accounts for almost $900, while the 8 per cent provincial tax is added to the sale price.
To sum up, the two governments once again recover $1,200 in all kinds of taxes, while the dealer who often has to fight competition must be satisfied with a small profit of $200.
Mr. Speaker, one thing that strikes Canadians more particularly: the ever increasing amounts of money they have to pay to service the national debt. If we want to compare, that is very easy when we know that the national debt of our country was only $75 million in 1867. This debt which had increased five-fold before World War I went up to more than $314 million to reach $1,500 million in the 20's. Then, we went through the depression and World War II; the debt of Canada which stood at more than $11 billion in 1945 reached $12 billion in 1960.
At page 22 of the 1973-74 issue of its booklet entitled: "How your tax dollar is spent", the Treasury Board gives the following explanation:
In March, 1972, at the close of the fiscal year, Canada's gross public debt, owed mainly to Canadians, stood at $48 billion.
And one can read a little further:
Paying the interest and other charges on this debt is going to cost $2,581 million in 1973-74.
Mr. Speaker, the estimates of government expenditures for the year 1964-65 showed that $1 billion were paid in interests on the public debt. In 1970-71, the then Minister of Finance gave a figure of $1,880 million for the public debt; and today, in the booklet I have referred to, we can find the amount of $2,500 million, that is $7 million a day only in interests on the national debt.
If one considers that there are about 22 million people in Canada and that interests must be paid on an amount of $2,500 million, this means approximately $110 a year per capita.

Therefore, it is good to recall that in 1945 the annual interest on the national debt was only $26 per capita. Within less than 30 years, this amount has increased fourfold. In my opinion, those are the results of the financial system to which this government and others before have faithfully adhered.
Mr. Speaker, we can read in the motion, and I quote:
That this House no longer has confidence in the government which, bu its weak and stubborn adherence to outmoded policies . . .
"By its weak adherence", Mr. Speaker, I am really opposed to that. And at present, this government is not working by weakness but it acts in collusion with the bankers and the Progressive Conservative Party. I shall take the liberty of telling how far such complicity could go. Let us remember March 1967, when the following motion was brought before the House:

Decennial revision and extension of charters
The house in committee on Bill No. C-222, respecting banks and banking-Mr. Sharp-Mr. Batten in the chair.
Mr. Speaker, the law in effect dated back to 1954. Such a law should have been revised in 1964, but as this lapse of time was not long enough for everybody to put his finger in the pie, I imagine, and because there were quite many elections that were really costly to the old parties, new legislation on banks was brought in to us in 1967, that is three years late. The old act provided a maximum interest of 6 per cent on loans given by banks and Bill C-222 meant to have such a maximum removed.
Mr. Speaker, it was a fantastic success. After a week of discussions, we got to the vote and page 14314 of Hansard indicates that 80 members were in favour of the bill and 40 were against it. That is where the scandal lay.
Mr. Speaker, at that time, there was really a great team: 97 Progressive Conservatives, while 40 per cent only voted against the elimination of the ceiling on interest on loans made by banks. If we except Creditists and Neo-Democrats, we realize that only 24 Progressive Conservatives members had the courage to vote, 73 having abstained.
Take the Creditists out-
You would have a better game-

It is really surprising. Even the right hon. Prime Minister of the time (Mr. Pearson) was not there. The hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand) and the hon. member for Quebec-East (Mr. Duquet) as well as those for Charlevoix, Drummond, Saint-Hyacinthe were not there; there were serious hon. members like those for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) who were not in the House. All these hon. members were among the gang of 73 who thought they had better hide behind the curtains.
Mr. Speaker, today the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is asking the government what it is going to do to prevent the rise in the interest rate. But there is

nothing to do because the bill has been passed. We have to wait until 1977, provided everything goes smoothly. So I find it ridiculous to wonder what we are going to do. All we had to do, was to vote against the bill and let the ceiling at 6 per cent. It is as simple as that.
At one point, realizing that the act had been enacted without anyone being the wiser for it, I sent out a circular in my riding, asking the following questions, and I quote:
Through what regional newspaper did you learn that the Bank of Canada Act was amended to allow the chartered banks to loan $100 with as little as a $7 reserve? (Bill C-190 passed by the House of Commons on March 15, 1967.)
Did those same newspapers, radio and TV stations controlled by the regular news services advise you that the ceiling on bank interest rates has been lifted for a period of 10 years? (Bill C-222, March 21, 1967.)
Over the next ten years, how much more will you have to pay for federal, provincial, municipal and school interests, as well as for your own personal affairs?
When we speak of inflation today, that is where we are at. We have the result of the votes expressed by the House of Commons.
Now, to resume my quotation:
DID YOU KNOW THAT ACCORDING TO THE CANADIAN CONSTITUTION, the Canadian government is the one which is supposed to set interest rates?
It should have been easy enough to oppose that particular bill that time. And I asked them the following question:
Do you know any other reason besides the electoral fund on which were based the many absences among the Conservatives?
Do you know some Liberal members who sought the advice of their electors before supporting that bill?
Our electors are asked to give their views on the death penalty but there is no way they will be asked to allow banks to deprive them of their money. I continue the quotation:
Considering that between 1944 and 1967 the assets of 8 chartered banks grew five-fold and that during the same period, the dividends paid by these banks went up from 6 to 30 per cent.
Do you think that it is urgent to let those institutions increase their profits and do you feel that the old parties have protected the thieves long enough?
Mr. Speaker, a bill to amend the Bank Act will be reintroduced automatically in 1977. But in the meantime, there is no ceiling and the banks can do as they please, with the results we already know, that is, an uncontrollable public debt.
Now, since the bankers have their spokesmen in Parliament, there are those among them who say that a public debt is a national blessing since it provides businessmen and financiers with a safe form of investment. Yet others, such as the hon. member for Langelier, who has already said as much in this House, state that a national debt does no harm to the country, since it is between fellow Canadians and that the money being spent to maintain this debt is changing pockets.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Minister of Transport should know that the pockets do not usually all belong to the same pair of trousers, nor to the same taxpayer.
The people in Canada who are drawing interest on the public debt of almost $2.5 billion that Canadians will have to pay in 1973, are not those in the lower income bracket.
Cost oi Living
On the contrary, the people drawing this interest are in the upper income bracket and a large proportion of the interest will simply go to fatten the bankers' dividends.
And I think that the word "system" is a rather weak one in view of the "jobbery" that is going on with the national finances. In short, the government, the so-called defender of the people, has become the largest collection agency, to the advantage of the money-lenders. In order to pay the interest on bank loans, the government is imposing more and more taxes of all kinds.
The financial statement of the Bank of Canada gives another proof that the Canadian citizen cannot obtain a strong percentage of the money used to say the national debt. For example, for the years 1957 to 1960, that financial statement showed that the credit created by banks represented 91.8 per cent whereas coins and paper money which can only be disposed of by citizens represented 8.2 per cent.
A Canadian authority on finance Mr. W. Trimble of the Ryerson Institute of Toronto wrote in his book:
We know already that the largest form of money is credit; and the greatest amount of credit is the credit created out of nothing by banks.
Banks lend people money that comes out of nowhere and goes back nowhere when the loan is paid off.
The greatest part of the revenue of banks comes from interests collected on money that does not exist.
So, Mr. Speaker, in order to pay its friends the bankers interest on money that did not exist, this government has a very well broken in tax machine: taxes on building materials, sales taxes on everything it sees and everything it foresees, special taxes, regular taxes of every imaginable kind, temporary taxes, special income taxes and excise taxes.
We also know that a research group is always working on new tricks and trying to find ways to have them swallowed.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that at all levels our governments have become all powerful collection agencies. But I am equally sure that the people of Canada agree that the government of Canada has become the top collector.
It is evident that for honestly administered cities and municipalities that collection job is most unpleasant. If municipal authorities admit it, it is with regret that they do it because they are forced to do it under the system.
For the federal government and the provincial governments, it is quite another thing. Collection which is done as satistically as possible has become the interesting point of their administration, the reward for which is this annual picnic commonly called the federal-provincial conference.
For the benefit of high finance, this picnic is repeated every year. In this summit meeting, they take pleasure in discussing sharing powers and tax fields. But never do they talk about finding cheap capitals or asking bankers to lower their rates of interest. People will be told to tighten their belt, the provinces will be urged to delay the implementation of important, essential projects but bankers will never be requested to bring down their rates of

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living
interest. No question about that, for how can those people be asked to do such things when we well know how generous they were during the election campaign?
At this kind of meeting, the participants invariably wonder which of the two governments, federal or provincial, will be the first to take the most from taxpayers' pockets. And every year we have the same situation. It is never resolved because there must be a good reason to levy new taxes.
Before saying that interest rates are too high, that finance has become too expensive, the federal government tells us: If we impose new taxes it is because we give provinces too much money.
Mr. Speaker, the interest presently charged by money and credit manufacturers is too high. They have even come up with bait policies in order to gain public acceptance. To force workers and farmers to borrow money, premiums are granted to them but those premiums are taken back the following day through taxes increases.
In order to prompt the industrialist to borrow for new equipment or for improving his business, a premium is offered to him in the form of a grant paid by several departments, as, for instance, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, but that kind of premium is rapidly written off by taxes collected on profits, if any, and by prohibitive interest rates that the businessman must pay on his current account and his mortgages.
Mr. Speaker, unduly high interest rates are the cause of many bankruptcies. Excessively high interest rates are one of the reasons why several Canadian industries have been forced to close down. Capital, which has been created to be used, has become a source of problems for the country; provinces, public corporations, everyone as a matter of fact, are in a bad position.
In studying the situation of our Canadian cities, we realize that the public debt has become the number one problem. Interests present 25 to 50 per cent and even 60 per cent of their budget.
The situation is the same in construction. Capital is granted to certain corporations, for instance to build homes for elderly people, but once such a home is built, we realize there is three homes to pay for: the one that was really built and two others to the financing institution.
And so it goes for housing. The worker is financed to build a house for terms as long as 25 to 30 years, and the worker realizes that he too will have to pay his house three times over. He had a single house built, but credit costs will be twice the price of his house.
So we wonder and seek the root of that evil. The reason is inflation, some say. Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, we have sufficient evidence: income tax at the source, various taxes hidden behind all goods we buy, municipal and school taxes; in fact, citizens have become slaves tied at both ends, a little like sausages.
Now, we pay twice or thrice what we received once. The situation is quite simple, and everybody understand that. The answer was also found long ago. But, in my opinion, our administrators act as if they were still looking for an answer, just to create jobs. There has been calculations,

there has been adjustments, and at the government's request, an ingenious device has been discovered.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion placed before the House today by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) does two things: it makes a point on a crucial matter and it implies a choice of an alternative. I shall touch on both those aspects. My hon. friend has covered a good deal of ground in making his presentation. I listened with interest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). In his reply he called attention to the approach being followed by the government-one attacking increases in prices by increasing supply.
But what has happened? The price of houses is up by 13 per cent this April as compared with a year ago. The government is pursuing a policy of increasing interest rates, a policy which is bound to have a dampening effect on the housing situation. Here the government is obvious-
<
June 14, 1973

ly involved in a contradiction. Any effort to fight inflation by increasing the supply of housing is already bogged down as a result of a patent contradiction in government policy.
Hear, hear!

The minister spoke about the introduction of lower taxes-a measure which six months ago he said would have bankrupted the country. He spoke about increasing old age pensions-which six months ago, he said, would bankrupt the nation. He said the same thing with regard to family allowances. Talk about changing positions, Mr. Speaker. Talk about weather vanes! I know of no one in this chamber, either in the front rows or in the back rows who could compare with the Minister of Finance when it comes to changing position.
Hear, hear!

Nobody need worry very much that the hon. gentleman rejects the policies we have advanced today, because, in view of the record of the minister in the last six months, he is very likely to adopt them tomorrow.
Oh, oh!

The minister says we on this side have grossly misjudged the economic situation. I have been making comments on the government's economic policy and on the economic situation, particularly since 19691970. I remember how the then minister of finance made fun of our prediction that unemployment would not fall below 6 per cent. I think that was in 1970 or 1971. Talk about misjudging the situation. But that does not bother the present Minister of Finance because he implicitly disavowed the policy followed by his predecessors in 1969, 1970 and 1971. I said we have been consistent since 1969 in advocating economic policies, and we have been right. To date, at least, the present Minister of Finance and his predecessors have been consistently wrong.
Hear, hear!

This is one thing that can be said without fear of successful contradiction. At the time the budget was brought down in February we advocated a two-fold thrust aimed at coping with unemployment, and we did, as part of that proposal, propose getting rid of the sales tax on building materials. We also recommended the removal of the sales tax not merely from children's clothing but from all clothing, both as a stimulant to the economy and as a measure designed to reduce costs. It was a two-fold proposal involving stimulation of the economy and a method of coping with inflation, in the belief that the people would wholeheartedly support such a proposal. The tragedy of the present situation is that the government has no adequate approach to dealing with inflation. The tragedy is that long before unemployment has fallen to acceptable levels, particularly in some areas of the country, and particularly among young Canadians, interest rates will have skyrocketed still higher and we shall once again go through what we went through before.
As to the government's methods, in February of this year the Minister of Finance stated that his budget would
Cost of Living
moderate inflation. In February the price level stood at 5.8 per cent above the level 12 months previously, and by May of this year it was 7.3 per cent higher than it was last May. In May of this year food for the family table cost over 15 per cent more than it did a year ago. But in spite of the evidence that the rate of inflation is accelerating in this country, the minister continues to rely on his obviously ineffective policies.
He speaks about the decreases he has made in excise taxes. At the time of the budget this reduction was to do great things to bring inflation under control. It has done so little to be effective that not only have the cost of living indices continued to rise but the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) has not had the courage to produce the report he said he would produce in respect of supervision and surveillance on the passing on of these tax cuts.
Hear, hear!

There is the true test of the effectiveness of the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). What did the government do? It set up a commission in respect of food prices-a commission that had no teeth. Anyway, you cannot tackle food prices by themselves. Last year the cost of farm production went up over 10 per cent in this country. In the first quarter of this year it again went up very substantially. You can only attack food prices across the board. I suppose that is why in its presentation on the budget the Canadian Federation of Agriculture said:
Our recent annual meeting of delegates declared in favour of the institution of wage and price controls supplementing broad fiscal and monetary policies. In the farmers' view, they have been and are among the losers, not the gainers-
Farmers recognize that the government will not adequately tackle food prices by appointing a toothless commission. If you are adequately to tackle food prices you must have a coherent policy and attack inflation right across the board. All we are getting from the present government's policies are higher prices and higher interest rates which will have disastrous effects for many Canadians.
In more recent days the government has shown the same wanton disregard for cost of living increases that it showed in previous days for unemployment increases. There is just no effective action being taken to restore order to the economy. One has to ask why, in light of the urgency of the problem, and at a time when we have an opportunity to pursue some parallel course with Great Britain-which is having more success in respect of its freeze than the minister likes to admit.
Where are the figures?

The figures are there, and they are considerably better than the hon. member likes to think. We have an opportunity now to tackle this problem. We urged that determined action be taken in February. We must keep asking ourselves why the Canadian government is so complacent. We believe that something can be done. We put our proposals forward in February. We said we should

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living
have a 90-day freeze on prices and incomes in order to break the chain of cost-price increases and in order to bring together the provinces, the producers, the unions and businessmen for consultation in respect of more selective controls, to be followed by what I would envisage to be a period of 18 months or two years wherein changes would be related to principles of productivity and cost.
We said we would have done this in conjunction with the tax cuts I mentioned-taking the sales tax off building material and taking all taxes off clothing. I am certainly not going to apologize for that. I want to emphasize that we are not talking about permanent controls. I have always believed, and still believe, that permanent price controls would destroy our market economy and simply result in vast power being centralized in the hands of a few officials and perhaps a few ministers here in Ottawa.
I have said, too, that I would not hesitate to resort to a temporary system of controls in order to prevent the inflationary psychology from accelerating rapidly throughout the economy. That is what I said last fall, and that is what I still believe. That is what we said in February when we were in the situation where a temporary freeze and a temporary set of controls were justified and necessary to head off an accelerating rate of inflation, a rate of inflation that has continued since we made that proposal. That proposal offered some possibility, not only of preventing the inflationary psychology from rapidly accelerating but it held some prospect of squeezing some of the inflationary expectations out of our economy.
Look at how much worse things are today. In the meantime, the government has been playing the old trade-off game. Interest rates have gone up, and the Minister of Finance's assurance about preferential treatment for Canadian borrowers is absurd. Other ministers are talking about food prices, housing prices and clothing prices in equally ridiculous terms. It is one thing to whistle in the dark when it is dark, but here we have a group that is in broad daylight putting on blindfolds and whistling in chorus.
Hear, hear!

Not everybody in the backbenches is whistling behind the fellows in the front benches, because on the government side frustration over the cabinet's complacency is growing. I think it was on May 10, about a month ago, that the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) rose in this House and spoke out in favour of a system of short-term controls. He knows something about agriculture and the effect of this proposal on agriculture. That was during a previous debate on the cost of living which my party had initiated. It may well be that in due course more government members will follow. As I said, before very long no doubt the Minister of Finance will be urging this himself as if he had invented the idea of having a freeze and controls.
He has not had an original thought for ten years.

After all, in the past couple of days we have seen other refreshing signs of outspokenness by some Liberal backbenchers, those who recognize perhaps that their party is more in need of medication than meditation.
Hear, hear!

I am sure some of them look at the front benches and wonder how much more upside down you can get. Whether we have any influence or effect on the government today, we can hope that the government will reverse itself on this matter as it has on so many others. I wonder just how bad things will have to become in the meantime; and even if the government does get around to adopting our position, I wonder how effective it will be when it really does not believe in the idea at all?
Some members to the left, particularly the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis)-
They are not here.
They have a representative here, Mr. Speaker.
It's a good job you don't have him to draft your motions.

I am a little puzzled by their comments on this matter because they seem to vacillate between sabre-rattling and support. This has been their pattern in respect of a food prices review board. I do not know today whether they are happy with it or not, and if they are not I do not know what they intend to do about it except to sit here and wait for somebody else to do something. In relation to housing costs and mortgage rates, evidently they think there should be selective controls. The member who spoke for them today suggested there should be certain selective controls. His leader was quoted today as saying that he wanted to do some further thinking about a freeze on food prices. That would seem to be going around, not only precisely in circles but in a good deal of confusion in trying desperately to find a policy which will in some way sound convincing.
There has been a lot of talk today about politics and about people adopting views which seem to be politically desirable. The hon. member for York South is fond of accusing me of being in bed with the business interests in this country. I wonder if he thinks the people in the corporate community are clamouring for a freeze or for short-term controls. I have not seen this mentioned in any brief from the chambers of commerce or from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
Or the CLC.

Or the CLC. Certainly, when it comes to the general public's interest regarding the terrible problems which exist in respect of the cost of living, it should be pretty evident that my party is not the rigid instrument which my friends to the left would like to make it out to be, and it should be evident that that party is more rigid than it is prepared to admit, although it seems to be breaking loose and moving around a bit in some confusion.
It is a fundamental purpose of allotted opposition days to air the urgent problems facing the country. Debate on these problems carries to the country the positions taken by the parties in parliament, including the government.
June 14, 1973

The government keeps explaining why things cannot be done. With the policies which this government has, I cannot see any hope of slowing down what is evidently an increasing rate of inflation in this country. Such debate reveals programs where they are present, inconsistencies where they exist, and complacency where it resides. We think all three are amply evident today: we have a program, there is the inconsistency of the NDP, and there is the government's complacency.
I should like to say a few words about the nature of the motion before us, the position of my party in putting forward this motin and the possible consequences of such a motion being adopted. The motion before us is a nonconfidence motion, with a vote tonight. Two such non-confidence motions in each supply period are provided by the rules of the House. It is the duty of the official opposition in this House to reflect the major concerns of the day in these non-confident motions so that the House may express an opinion on the government's performance. The obligation of the official opposition in a minority House is not only to use these occasions to express displeasure with the government but to indicate an alternative course. If the government is defeated on such a non-confidence vote, then the official opposition stands ready to form a government and put its alternative into legislation and into practice.
Hear, hear!

I would remind the House and my hon. friends to the left that it is the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who has taken the line that a defeat on legislation which went to the root of government principles would necessitate an election. It is the Prime Minister who took that position, and it is the Prime Minister's interpretation that the government itself decides, after the fact, whether or not any matter has gone to the root of its so-called principles.
Since this parliament commenced it is the Prime Minister, not me, who has indicated that no one could prevent dissolution, in any event, if he wished it. The Prime Minister says in essence: If you don't want an election, then it is up to the opposition parties to somehow give the government what the voters refused to give it last October 30 the comfort of a majority in the House of Commons.
The leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for York South, has taken the position that he and his group would support the government so long as what the government did was satisfactory in their eyes. I took from what I heard today that the government's performance in respect of inflation is not satisfactory in the eyes of the New Democratic Party members. Their position has not presumed the necessity of an election to change the government: quite the contrary, it is the Prime Minister who took that position.
On the subject matter before us today we have fulfilled our responsibility in terms of putting forward an alternative. We have indeed put forward an entire package of alternative economic policies. We stand ready, if called upon, to form a government and take action. We have always been prepared to face this parliament on the basis of policies we have put before the people, and the policies we continue to put before the people, rather than, like this
Cost of Living
government, face this House on policies virtually the opposite to those on which it ran the election.
Hear, hear!

We were ready when we outlined our alternatives in the budget debate. In the four months since then the need for our alternative has become more and more evident, and the government's complacency and lack of success in dealing with inflation has become more and more intolerable. So, Sir, I seek support for our motion on the basis that inflation is rapidly escalating and that the predictions and promises of the Minister of Finance show the ineffectiveness of these band-aid programs to deal with inflation. These programs have consistently been proven wrong and the rate of inflation has consistently moved upward. I say that action must be taken, and I seek support for our motion on the basis that we on this side of the House are prepared to act in response to the urgent problem of inflation. We have placed a program before the people, and we are prepared to act now.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I do not profess to have the oratorical prowess of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). Nevertheless, I think we can come to grips with the problem in a little better manner, get away from some of the rhetoric and get down to some of the basic problems facing the House. First of all, in respect of the statement which has been made about frustration among the backbenchers of the government party, let it be very clear that not only was I not handed a prepared speech but I was given no indication of how I should frame my remarks.
Try defecting.

Then there was the statement that some of us may be dissatisfied with inflation. I think all of us are. But the suggestion that we are dissatisfied with the action this government has taken on inflation is a different matter entirely. None of us likes what is happening at the present time, but we must keep things in some sort of perspective in a country where purchasing power is rising at a rate probably faster than at any time since the war. In this situation we find ourselves being led voluntarily into a position where we are buying more and more of various commodities, where we are getting a higher quality product and are prepared to pay more as a consequence.
On a typical day we start the morning with breakfast, for which we have canned, reconstituted orange juice and quick oats: we do not boil oatmeal over a slow fire any more. The kids have cold cereal done up in fancy, small packages. We have eggs. We know what has happened to the price of eggs because we have run into a shortage of feedstuffs. As for mushrooms, we are growing more mushrooms than ever in the history of this country. The price of mushrooms is skyrocketing because of the demand; we love to eat them. Then we have instant coffee, or tea using flowthrough teabags.
I will dwell for a moment on the staple food which we have with our breakfast, namely, bread. The other day we

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living
were discussing the fact that this year we negotiated the sale of some 200 million bushels of wheat at a price which is generally agreed to be in the order of $2.60 a bushel. The price last year was $1.70 a bushel. The question naturally arises: What is the effect on the price of a loaf of bread? The answer to that is, zero. Why is that so? It is not that the farmer will receive more for his wheat, but the taxpayer is paying a subsidy to ensure that the price of a loaf of bread is not increased because export prices are rising. I suggest this indicates something we could do which has not been suggested by the opposition, namely, have the taxpayers subsidize the cost of food.
There are other alternatives. One weekend Japan decided to stop importing our pork and during that weekend the price of pork dropped from $1.05 a pound to 80 cents a pound. It follows, therefore, that we could reduce the price of pork by stopping our exports. I suggest that this would have exactly the reverse effect in the long run, since the farmer, making less profit, would tend to turn to other products thus creating, eventually, a shortage of the product, which would drive the price up to where it was originally.
We are demanding more and more foods in prepared form, such as frozen French fries and frozen vegetables of all kinds. While we are on the subject of vegetables, I notice that the price of onions has risen by some 50 per cent. However, I will not concern myself with that matter, because now my best friend will not need to warn me; the price situation will take care of the problem! We buy quick desserts, such as canned rice-pudding. We buy high-priced, high-quality frozen pies and cakes, and more and more as we demand high-quality, prepared foods in a form for which we have never previously asked, we naturally remove from the market the cheaper foods required by the lower income groups.
Our concern in foodstuffs must be not for the middle-income and high-income groups, but for those with low incomes who are not able to cope with increases in food prices. This government has already taken firm steps to put a little more money into the pockets of those with low incomes by increasing old age pensions and by reductions in taxes to compensate them for the higher cost of living.
I want to deal for a moment with the cost of housing, and particularly the cost of lumber. At the moment we are exporting lumber. The opposition has suggested that it is the exporting of lumber which is creating shortages, resulting in higher prices. I should point out that in the 1960s-and after all, which country has greater access to lumber than Canada-despite the large quantities of lumber available in this country we found that lumber companies were going broke. Those that survived were making negligible profits. Only very recently has the price of lumber risen to the point where lumber companies are starting to make reasonable profits.
Quite obviously we can, once again, by not exporting reduce the price of lumber, which would reduce the cost of housing. However, since we are now building houses at a rate faster than ever before in our history-some 273,000 units per annum; some 70,000 odd units per annum more than is considered essential by the Economic Council of Canada-I am not sure that the price of lumber, even

though it is going up, is in any way acting as a deterrent in the construction of housing.
When we consider the price of housing we always look at the high cost in areas where, because of shortage of land and high labour rates, the cost of land has escalated more than it has generally across the country. In Toronto at present, where the average citizen prefers to live in a single family residence, the spread of the city has created a shortage of land to the point where the land that is available has increased substantially in price. Little mention is made of the fact that in and around the city of Montreal, which is equal in size to Toronto but where living habits are different-in contrast to Toronto where two-thirds of the population live in single family residences, two-thirds of the residents of Montreal live in apartments-there is land available.

speechtext:
Order. Before recognizing the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) who had the floor at six o'clock, I wish to return to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin). Before inviting hon. members to make a contribution on the procedural aspects, may I say that I am just about ready to let the amendment be put to the House, for reasons that I will explain.

Hon. members know that the Chair indicated, when the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) moved his motion before the House adjourned at six o'clock, that it would be willing, at eight o'clock to hear the arguments on whether or not it is in order.
I must say, at this point, that I am very reticent, from the procedural point of view about accepting the amendment in its present form. First of all, the first part of the amemdment does not, to my mind, alter the main motion, and referring hon. members to Beauchesne's citation 202(15), the Chair should, normally, reject an amendment which, all in all, would only confirm what is already stated in the main motion.
The greatest difficulty arises about the second part of amendment. Indeed, the proposal of the hon. member for Portneuf is an entirely new motion whose object is not anticipated in the main motion.
The Chair is reluctant to accept such an amendment, because we are holding today a debate on a non-confidence motion in the government. Still the mover has the privilege of choosing the subject matter of his motion and if one is allowed to introduce amendments deviating from the subject, even if it deals with a related field, those amendments are entirely different proposals and I think
June 14, 1973

that it is an abuse of the privileges granted to the mover of the main motion.
This being said, I think that hon. members can find all the arguments concerning such a decision which could be reached in the citations from Beauchesne, citation 203, paragraphs (1), (3) and (5).
According to me, the second part of the amendment presented by the hon. member for Portneuf should normally require previous notice which should have appeared on the order paper, but anyway, in the circumstances, that point will not influence my decision. I only want to warn hon. members against the danger of allowing that kind of procedural laxity, particularly in the case of a non-confidence motion, a laxity from which the first to suffer would be hon. members who, occasionally, wish to propose such non-confidence motions.
However, we are today holding a debate of utmost importance because the matter discussed is after all basic in terms of the existence or survival of a government and instead of using a period of 30 to 60 minutes for procedural discussion, inviting hon. members to enlighten the Chair and reach a final decision, I deemed in all justice and equity for those who have presented the main motion, I ought to accept the amendment while restating however my doubts concerning its form, and particularly concerning the terms of the second part of the said amendment.
Considering those reserves, and at the same time while warning hon. members, I, therefore, intend to accept the amendment and submit it to the House.
Mr. Godin, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), moved to amend the main motion by adding, immediately after "living increases", the following:
"and because it has not given consideration to financial reforms which would have made it possible to fight against price increases and inflation by enforcing the following economic principles:
The compensated discount and the issue of new credits by the Bank of Canada to finance all new projects."
The hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert).

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Order, please. Before making my ruling, I should have apologized for interrupting the hon. member who was supposed to have the floor at eight o'clock. The Chair will surely take this into account in the time allotted to the hon. member and will listen to him most closely.

Mr. Speaker, I am wondering if I should change my mind now, on account of the amendment, but- [English]
Mr. Speaker, when the House recessed at six o'clock we had been discussing rising prices and I was speaking specifically about housing. I wondered why references to housing costs all seemed to centre around costs in Toronto, when other big cities such as Montreal have not suffered the same problems as Toronto because land is available
Cost of Living
and housing can be built at a lower cost. Good treed land is available at the moment at 25 cents per square foot in the whole of the area around Montreal, and one can build a house in the $14,000 to $16,000 bracket. As many houses are being built there as in Toronto, which indicates to me that houses can be purchased at prices within the means of Canadians if people do not insist on building in downtown locations where the cost of land is, admittedly, very high.
We must also realize, when talking about housing costs, that these days people are demanding a much higher standard in house construction than used to be the case. They are demanding parquet flooring, ceramic tiled bathrooms, electrical outlets, for example, to service various electrical appliances which are two or three times the size of those installed some 20 years ago. They expect all kinds of landscaping, sidewalks, carports, finished basements, and so on. So we are not comparing apples with apples. Even so, today, more than 25 years after the war, we can still see houses being built for less than double the price that obtained in the late forties and early fifties. This, to me, is not an unreasonable price increase, especially when one takes into account the difference in the quality of the product being purchased.
When the Leader of the Opposition was suggesting once again that the sales tax should be taken off building materials, having spent 25 years after the war in the construction industry I asked myself what real effect this would have on house construction. One thing is quite obvious: the benefit would be twice as much for the person building a $40,000 house than for the person building a $20,000 house. I wonder if that is what we are trying to achieve? We must remember that for most people it is the amount of the down payment that is important. For lower cost houses in the $14,000 to $20,000 bracket the down payment in many cases is still less than $1,000. I think this is very important, because finding the initial payment is the real cruncher. So long as house building continues at its present rate, and so long as people in the middle thirties age bracket are able to buy houses-as they are, in large numbers, across this country at the present time- then I do not think the situation is quite as grim as it is sometimes painted.
Another matter which is of concern to us at the present time is transportation. We know that commuter services are being used less and less. But compare prices, again. We know that a commuter today is paying about three times as much as 25 years ago on public transportation, but he is not using it; he is driving in and out of the city by private car, and he is generally driving alone. His costs are about three times what they would be if he used public transportation. In other words, despite higher costs, he uses what for him is a more convenient form of transportation and he chooses to pay more.
The Leader of the Opposition again referred to his suggested 90-day freeze on prices and incomes. Again, we are not talking about freezing prices at the farm gate, and there is no suggestion as to what will happen between the price at the farm gate level and the pegged price at the retail level. The freeze is suggested in order to bring everybody together for consultation. I wonder what we have been doing over the last few months, Mr. Speaker. We have consulted here in committee, we have had consul-

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living
tations across the country, and the media has discussed what we should do. I suggest that we have had enough consultation. We do not need a 90-day freeze in order to give us the opportunity to consult.
I find suggestions in that respect quite barren. We have had discussions; we do not need a freeze for purposes of consultation. Therefore, we must examine the real motivation behind the suggestion. It is a nice, pat answer to give when talking about freezing prices; it sounds good. We have seen what has happened in the United States. They are faced with the situation today where the President has once again been obliged to impose some controls. We ask ourselves: If it applies in the United States, why should it not apply here? I think we forget that as a major exporting and importing nation we are far more subject to the influence of price on our imports than is the United States. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I suggest we are not in a position to compare ourselves with the United States in this respect.
I also believe, as was said earlier, that to some extent the President was forced into the decision he took yesterday, He did this as a sort of diversionary tactic, because obviously the situation in the United States calls for action by the government to take the heat off the economy. That does not apply in this country. We do not need these diversionary tactics. If we are to apply any price control, we should do it for a specific reason knowing full well what the effect will be on the consumer. Unless we realize that the imposition of price and wage controls today will lead to greater price increases when the controls are eventually taken off, as they must be, we are only kidding ourselves in the interim.
I listened with great interest to members on the other side of the House, because even though they sometimes refer to us as a bunch of penguins-I think that is the term they use-
Trained seals.

Trained seals, that's it. Even though that is how they refer to us, we do try to find good ideas. We would use them if we could find them. To date we are finding few ideas coming from the other side that would tend to make us change our minds.

speechtext: How many of our ideas have you used until now?

I am strongly opposed to controls. At the moment, labour in this country is making reasonable demands. If we try to impose controls we will only make labour dissatisfied, and without controls on labour any kind of controls at the retail price level would be completely ineffective. Also, one cannot impose controls at the retail level without considering controls at the farm level, for they would be equally ineffective. I think the whole idea just does not make sense. That is why I intend to vote against the motion.

Mr. Speaker, we are engaged in a debate on an extremely important

motion which leaves nobody indifferent and boils down to condemning this government because it persists stubbornly in applying outmoded measures which oppress the people of Canada with ever more painful increases in the cost of living.
Something both tragic and disconcerting must be pointed out in this debate.
On the one hand, the official opposition does its duty and under the rules of this House tells the government what the people of the country think about the policy followed up to now by this government.
On the other hand, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), instead of putting forward the future policy of the government which should at least bring some relief to the people of this country oppressed by the cost of living, devotes a lot of his time to ridiculing the opposition, criticizing in a negative way, using sarcasms and, in short, keeping from telling members of this House about the future policy of this government.
However, a third party, the New Democratic Party, through its spokesman, openly admitted that it will vote against that motion, that it will refuse to condemn this government because according to them the time has not come for an election campaign.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, one could read today in an editorial in La Presse, a suggestion by a very well informed editorialist Mr. Jean Pellerin who in the past has always had high praise for the merits of this government, and I quote:
As though from evil thoughts, Ottawa shies away from the very idea of freezing prices and wages, even for a limited time, in order to take the time to find the cause of the trouble and restrain voracious appetites. The taxpayer feels helpless. If governments, not satisfied with doing nothing to check price increases, go so far as to shamelessly contribute to it, who will ever be able to restore some order in this area?
Mr. Speaker, this is what we find disconcerting. We are all worried and we wonder why the government does not show leadership in an area so essential to our country. And yet, statistics are there and I think they speak for themselves. Last month, consumers were greatly shocked by the cost of living figures. If we figured the annual rate, we would notice that the consumer price increase was 12.1 per cent and that in the food index-what a tragedy for underfed people!-it was 31.2 per cent.
The substantial increases in the cost of living in May, published on June 12 by Statistics Canada, confirmed too tragically the size of the problem. One has to go back to 1948 to see, in May, such sadly spectacular jumps in the cost of living.
Mr. Speaker, in view of those facts and of such prospects, it is morally forbidden for us in this House to be satisfied with mere studies or often useless comparisons with other industrialized countries or, worse still, with statements from worn-out members playing politics or from clowns, as is often the case with the member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). Recently, during his spectacle, he was trying demagogically to find fault with the distinguished leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield), but unfortunately he could not distinguish between
June 14, 1973

our objective "galloping inflation brake" and our objective "better distribution among the people of the federal government spending power".
Mr. Speaker, while the federal Creditistes, to the amazement of Quebecers, keep on, as we noticed this afternoon, talking nonsense or refusing to give their opinion on matters of such importance as bilingualism, flirting dangerously with those they blame outside the House or spreading their rubbish on hot lines or elsewhere, while the government pretends to be studying, there are families in Saint-Hyacinthe, in the province of Quebec or elsewhere which can no longer feed themselves properly or have to spend a large part of their income to buy food.
Let us open our eyes on the figures of the cost of living. They make you think and think bluntly. So, for the period of April 1972 to April 1973 you will realize-and it comes out of a study made by the Pitfield, Mackay, Ross and Company brokerage firm-what a good investment the meat industry is. Poultry prices rose 26 per cent; beef prices increased by more than 16 per cent; pork prices went up by more than 30 per cent and egg prices jumped by 43 per cent. On the other hand, in Quebec City alone- it has been established by a scientific study-food prices rose 19 per cent within a two-year period.
And now experts tell us that enormous increases in soyabean prices this month on the Chicago market are going to cause meat and egg prices to rise sharply in the coming weeks. And in the area of soya production alone, the government is not even ready to develop a serious production policy which, in the medium and the long run, would make us independent or at least less slaves to the American market.
It appears clearly, Mr. Speaker, that this government, which is wanting in audacity, is incapable of resolving the alarming problem posed by the unrestrained increase in the cost of living.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, it is time for the government to step in efficiently and firmly. Is it always necessary to wait before acting that the less favoured in our society, particularly the poor and often numerous families grow sick and tired of being under-fed, under-housed and come to protest at our doors? Is that what we are waiting for?
As far as we are concerned, we honestly believe that the solutions we propose are striking at the heart of the problem and we are all the more confident because the party currently and temporarily in office has borrowed several of them since January 4, although criticizing them at the beginning, but there are a few examples of measures accepted by the current government. I am thinking about the adjustments in the tax deductions, the increase in the old age pensions and family allowances, the cost of living escalation in tax assessment and the elimination of the Benson injustice in the field of inheritance of family farms.
In fact this is understandable. It is because we are ready to govern this country whereas for the government people it is only a matter of time; they are getting ready to occupy the opposition benches even though in order to be noticed there they will again need the NDP veterans.
Let our position be clearly understood in Quebec as elsewhere in this country.
Cost of Living
First, we have been advocating for quite sometime a more expansionist budgetary and economical policy than that contained in the budget of February last. Our position in this connection is already well known particularly as regards the increased assistance to small businesses. It is our own way of fighting what has been called the "stagflation".
Secondly, we want the immediate freezing, but for 90 days only, of all prices and all kinds of income with the realistic exception of the raw food commodities at the farm gate.
This period would allow the government, after it has regained proper leadership, to consult thoroughly and negotiate seriously with the provincial governments, management and unions. Such an exchange of views in the interest of consumers would be aimed at developing, by means of a sudden check of the rampant inflation, a coordinated and exhaustive price and cost stabilization program. Such exchanges would already be made easier at the outset by the most relevant suggestions especially from the Alberta government, the UPA or the Canadian Consumers Association.
The advocated temporary freeze would surely create a beneficial psychological effect on inflation which also has psychological causes. However, such a freeze would not really cause panic because panic already exists among consumers who come to grips daily with excessive prices.
In the light of this clear-cut policy, the position of government members is for us a great cause for concern. The Minister of Finance would wait for the effect of his budget measures or of his so-called new programs. He is running the risk of waiting in vain, the effectiveness of such measures being concurrently drowned in the inflationary spiral.
According to a Gallup poll-and here I am not referring to the poll showing a loss of popularity for the Social Credit or the New Democratic parties or a slight increase in popularity for the Liberals neither even the increase, not assumed but real, of four points in favour of the Progressive Conservative party, but of a Gallup poll the results of which, were published on June 6 last and showed that 85 per cent of Canadians anticipate that prices will rise faster than the family income. That explains why previously, at least 61 per cent of the population had stated that they were in favour of controls on prices and incomes.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), in his statements to the farmers, seems to wish-and I concur-to give a new impetus to agriculture, but at the price-and this I find unacceptable-of inflation.
This reminds us, Mr. Speaker, of the not so distant time when this same government was attempting to stifle inflation at the price of a higher unemployment rate. The Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), doubtless in between putting coats of paint on his letter boxes, launches into smooth statements, and I am not referring to his statements on feed grain made in Drummondville last night, when he apparently substituted for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who in turn was to have substituted for the Minister of Transport (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
