Marchand) who was to have substituted for the Minister of Agriculture, who was probably to have substituted for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Corriveau).
The Postmaster General said on January 22, and I quote:
The government. . .
That is playing politics.

Speaking of playing politics, Mr. Speaker, I have also been informed that the Postmaster General travelled to Drummondville on a government aircraft, accompanied by nine Liberal members, without inviting any opposition members to accompany him.
Does that surprise you?

That surprises us; we will come back to that later, when the public accounts are being examined.
On January 22, our suave Postmaster General said:
The Canadian government pays special attention to the steps taken by other countries, like the United States, for instance.
Then, I ask him today if he will pay the necessary attention to the price freeze in the United States announced last night by President Nixon.
The same minister-responsible for stamps-said on April 16, and I quote:
The government will announce shortly a detailed plan of action- and so on.
And I ask him today if he believes that the mere fact of setting up a toothless commission is this detailed plan he had promised to the people. Finally, this suave Postmaster General, surely at a loss for inspiration, asserted on May 21, and I quote:
In the face of danger, the government remains calm.
No wonder it is calm, Mr. Speaker, it is so calm as to be disconcerting, and surely the first political boss of the Postmaster General, whom I knew quite well by the way, would flush with anger today if he heard these confusing statements of the hon. member for Papineau.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to warn the government members. Their attitude-
Exclamation mark.

And points of suspension.
Their present attitude in the face of the ever increasing cost of living, especially food, while they are satisfied with putting forward in a disorderly manner income support or replacement measures, not only unduly delays a healthy coordination of social security measures as well as the implementation of the guaranteed minimum income program, but also destroys initiative and encourages laziness and dependency, "demotivates" the ever forgotten ones of our country, namely the so-called middle class people and, finally, maintains a psychology of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, it is high time this government acted with firmness, coherence and swiftness to deal with the scandalous increase in the cost of living. The government should act or resign. Should it resign, it would only be confirming legally what it has been doing in effect,

namely resigning in the face of the alarming problems which oppress the people of Canada.
And all the time lost by this government postponing its decision places it in an increasingly incoherent situation and exposes it to an increasingly obvious loss of credibility and, of course, puts it on the road to defeat that some humorists, and perhaps some toady editorialists, will say in their headlines: "Because of the meat."
That is hypothetical!

If the Liberals, Mr. Speaker, once said about their colleagues of the New Democratic Party that they were basically Liberals in a hurry, which is less and less evident today, I say of the Liberals, which is more and more evident, that they have become Progressive Conservatives not in a hurry, not the least bit in a hurry.
Mr. Speaker, let us finally have a concerted plan to curb inflation! Let us have many, realistic, simultaneous and cohesive measures to deal in the general interest with the increase in the cost of living. If the government does not change radically, it will be repudiated by the people who in turn will say what we are saying today about that motion:
-this House no longer has confidence in the government which, by its weak and stubborn-
Amen!

-adherence to outmoded policies, increasingly burdens the people of Canada with grievous cost of living increases. '
-and the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) says: Amen!

Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in commenting on the motion and, at the same time, on the matter we are debating today in the House.
Undoubtedly, the matter we are discussing is of very special interest to all Canadians. We have been talking about the cost of living for a very long time and, of course, people are expecting that quite efficient measures will be taken to put an end to such a rise. There is no doubt whatever on that, and I think that all hon. members wish that some legislation will finally restrain these increases which are making life difficult for the Canadians.
The motion under study reads as follows:
That this House no longer has confidence in the government which, by its weak and stubborn adherence to outmoded policies-
-well, these views are slightly political-
-increasingly burdens the people of Canada with grievous cost of living increases.
I think that those last lines must hold the attention of the hon. members. There is no doubt that the cost of living increase is burdening the Canadian people. With objectivity, I am making these comments and inviting all members to consider the problem facing the Canadian people.
Surely, some members have spoken and have puffed their goods; I have heard up to now the views of some representatives of the four political parties. I think that
June 14, 1973

we cannot deny the cost of living increase is a basic problem and while acknowledging that the government has made many efforts during the past five or six years and that it is trying to solvp that problem, I honestly believe and I must admit that we did not succeed in checking the rise in the cost of living.
Now, we will try to justify ourselves by saying every so often: Well, the United States are not any better off than we are, or still, it is worse over there. Europe also has problems. The whole wide world has problems. Should we be content to look down on the difficulties experienced by other nations and say: Well, at home, the situation is not any worse off than elsewhere. On the contrary, I think we have reasons to believe and to hope that our government will find a solution to the extent that they will be ready and willing to accept some of the opinions voiced by members of the other parties in this House; but then, these opinions and suggestions must be effective.
Therefore, to that extent, I think the motion before us is rather a just one, although it may have political undertones-personally, I do not care-but we must admit that the cost of living has been rising constantly these last few years, that the government has found no adequate solution. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is nothing but the plain truth.
While I was listening to a member of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, I felt really disappointed by his party's attitude. Of course, they must make their position clear in case this government is overthrown. To begin with, I should like to tell the House that a government which would be defeated on such a motion would have no reason to resign. No, I suggest that, whenever the government does the right thing, it is our duty, as members of this House, to congratulate and support them. I, for one, have tried to find causes to do so for the past six years and have often succeeded. However, when they deserve to be blamed, it is our duty to do so and to remind them that the Canadian people is anxious anxiously waiting for a solution to their problem which bothers me considerably.
The government, which is eager to justify its actions, which is eager, by all sorts of means, to impress upon us that it has failed to find any solution, did not suggest that it could not find any or that it does not have it at present. I doubt that any other political party has it. Nobody will say that, but my position allows me to say that. I-
Speak for yourself!

Yes, Sir, I speak for myself, and I think that the Social Credit Party of Canada does certainly not have it either.
So, Mr. Speaker-
That is what you say!
The hon. member for Roberval reminds me that that is what I say, and that is what I think!
One cannot keep you from thinking that!

No, you certainly cannot stop me from thinking along these lines. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we
Cost of Living
acknowledge an accomplished fact: the solution which could be brought forth has not been submitted to us.
Mr. Speaker, I do not have that solution myself, in contrast with my friends to the right who think they have it, and, as a Frenchman said to a Creditiste member a year after his visiting Paris: Tell me, Dumont, your contraption, is it still working?
Bernard Dumont.

Yes, precisely.
I said a while ago that I was disappointed at the New Democratic Party's attitude, concerning the risk and peril of overthrowing the government. I do not think that a motion merely acknowledging a truth, if it were agreed to, would require the government to resign. Not at all. I do not believe that the government would lack the proper support. As for the mandatory legislation which of course is useful and clearly needed, I believe the government will have to decide whether or not he should go to the people. But it is not because the government is defeated on a motion of non-confidence that it should resign. I think that this Parliamentary tradition has already cost us enough. A government has every reason to continue to govern a country, even though it may be accused at one time of some weakness and of a lack of solutions, a thing we can also be said of all parties.
The attitude of the NDP, which refuses to support this motion, is really scandalous. Afraid to set off an election! One should not be so naive. I wonder what the supporters of the New Democratic Party, who saw these men fight the government as no one else did six months ago, must think of their elected representatives' attitude to so self-evident a truth, namely that the cost of living increase has not been slowed down. And it will be said: because they didn't want to support the Progressive Conservative Party, or, above all, because they didn't want to defeat the government. The New Democrats know just as well as I do that this in no way forces the government to go to the people. In my opinion, they realize that this lack of a solution will cause the government to work harder, to devote itself to finding a solution and perhaps to consider some of the suggestions that have been made.
As far as the construction sector is concerned, for example, a lot has been said about costs; there has been talk of abolishing the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. I spoke about that two years ago. The subject is still a current one and I believe the three opposition parties are calling for that removal.
We know very well that the complete removal of the 11 per cent sales tax would probably not bring about the expected benefits. The mere removal of the 11 per cent tax would represent a loss of revenue for the government. However, we know full well that the manufacturer of materials and the contractor would be tempted to profit by such a removal. Therefore the owner would not benefit by it.
Two years ago, I asked the government, to invite to the bargaining table unions, manufacturers of building materials and provincial governments in order to find a solution, to discuss together a policy that could be effective and would result in a price freeze for building materi-

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living
als. The government could say they are prepared to increase their credits so that the housing units could increase more rapidly than they do at the present time, in so far as the unions are willing to cooperate, insofar as they are willing to suspend the right to strike so as not to interfere with the building industry.
I believe that we should come as soon as possible to a comprehensive policy to that effect, but at one condition only, namely that the government invite at the same table all the people concerned in the building industry. The very removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials would not bring about the desired effects, but a comprehensive policy that would be well thought-out, well structured, and well negotiated with the responsible people in the building field would enable the government I think, to cope with conditions that have become very awkward for new owners.
As regards the price and wage freeze, one must still consider it before rejecting it off-hand. It is clear that reference is made to a 90-day price freeze. In my opinion, that period of time would be sufficient to find a solution. However, to freeze prices at their present level would do a disservice to the people in the long run.
It is obvious, and I said it three weeks ago, that to freeze the price of beef at 90 cents a lb. would suit Canada Packers Limited, but I think that it is also quite important to consider the matter and find a solution during those 90 days in order to reduce prices and it is not easy.
To what extent is the taxpayer responsible for that situation, Mr. Speaker? It is easy to blame the government or the legislators in that connection.
To what extent did the consumer himself contribute to the prices skyrocketting, prompted by the legitimate desire to acquire almost everything? To what extent does the government share that responsibility? The minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs might encourage more restraint on the part of the consumer. And I know that amongst opposition members publicity is made to encourage consumers to acquire the things that their neighbours have or that are common in other countries.
Then, the individual and not only the government must be educated in that respect. But in view of the problem, I think it is a real nonsense and a pity that certain members or political parties make out of this a partisan or political question. Canadian people are concerned; they want to see this problem dealt with as soon as possible and for this they rely upon the government.
As a matter of fact, members have the responsibility to discuss this question in a very objective manner and try to find a solution.
I think that the proposals which have been made deserve the attention of every member and that the motion under study which recognizes the fact that we did not succeed in reducing the rising cost of living is perfectly justified. Then, under the circumstances if I were to vote against that motion I would say in short that the government has succeeded in controlling inflation but it would be wrong. I do not say it is the fault of the government, alone because, as I have said before, the government has made enormous but inadequate efforts and I think this is the cause of the problem.

The Social Credit moved an amendment. I do not quite agree with the monetary theory of the Social Credit; therefore it is obvious that I will not vote for this amendment. There are people who believe in it. I do respect their opinion, as I respect all religions in this country; therefore I also respect the Social Credit. Personally, I do not believe in it. Of course, they will argue and do their best to prove that we have tried many things with the present system and they will say: why not try the monetary theory of the Social Credit? More people will have to believe in it before I am convinced. It is certainly not the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) who will convince me. I know too much about his ideas and arguments to be convinced. I must say there are some serious members in that party and I do respect them very much.
I think it is a question of principle. We have a motion before us and it deserves the attention of the House. We must not believe that the government would be defeated because it is a non confidence motion supported by the majority; rather I think we must remind the government that there is a serious problem in Canada and that it should try to do better than it is doing now.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to quote, as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) did a little while ago, what Mr. Pellerin of La Presse wrote about the New Democratic Party: It reads as follows:
The leader of the NDP, Mr. David Lewis, holds the Minister of Finance responsible for the price increase. He says that Mr. Turner maintains the price index at an artificially high rate because he intends to maintain the equivalence between the Canadian dollar and the American dollar. The explanation may seem far fetched but it might have some element of truth. However, in the eyes of ordinary people, it is thought there is a plot. Producers, packers, deliverers, merchants, proprietors, entertainment enterprises and even governments do nothing to stop price increases.
He ends by saying:
If prices carry on increasing at the present rate, the defence of common wealth will have to come before the respect of private enterprise. Inflation is threatening us all. The authorities must do something instead of washing their hands or taking advantage of the situation.
I believe that this final remark of this journalist deserves to be pondered over. I also think of the concern which the Canadian people has for this problem and I hope that today's debate will help us become even more alive to this problem and that we shall be united rather than divided in our search for its solution.
I believe this is the kind of objectivity which the people is looking for in the members of this House. For my part, such is the purpose I am serving here in this House and I believe it to be my duty and my responsibility to urge those members to work harder at finding the most beneficial solution for society and not a solution which is liable to bring about some political advantage at the polls.
Those who worry only about electoral advantages run the risk of being severely judged by their fellow-citizens who see them in action. Therefore, not only must the government do something but they must also act in the best interest of society. I hope that all these speeches will be followed by an effective and efficient application of the required measures so that we may at last stop the escala-
June 14, 1973

tion of the cost of living and give Canadians more hope than now in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate in support of the Progressive Conservative motion. It relates to a most urgent subject, namely, the absolute failure of the government to cope with the real problems which face the Canadian people at this time. It relates in particular to the stubborn adherence of the government to outmoded methods and outmoded policies. The government has tried by traditional means to meet the dual problems of unemployment and inflation and has failed miserably. There is no question whatsoever that monetary and fiscal policies alone will not do the job. Not in a dozen years will that approach adequately meet the needs of the Canadian people. If the government proceeds as it has, we will just move back and forth from too much unemployment to too much inflation, and too much of both, as has been the case these last few years.
It is perfectly obvious that something new must be added, and that is an incomes policy, particularly in the rigid sector of our economy, if we are to be able to cope with the real needs of the ordinary people of this country. In the face of this obviously serious situation, what is the government's response? It is virtually zero. It sets up a food prices commission. The head of that commission just the other day, almost immediately after she was appointed, was apologizing publicly for the government. She said that the people of Canada did not want controls. At least that was her opinion, Mr. Speaker.
How does she know?

My hon. friend asks, how does she know? That is the question which came to my mind at once. I wondered to whom she had been talking. Perhaps she had been talking to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce; perhaps she had been talking to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association; perhaps she had been talking to the Canadian Labour Congress; or perhaps she had been talking to the cabinet. One thing is sure, Mr. Speaker; she was not talking to the Canadian people, to the average citizen of this country.
Hear, hear!

As far as I know, in every poll sent out by any member of this House of Commons in the last year or year and a half in which members' constituents have been polled on their attitude toward wage and price controls, the answer has been in the affirmative. Even in the case of one hon. member opposite who sent a questionnaire to his constituents on the Island of Montreal, where the question was framed in this way, "Would you favour wage and price controls even if it meant a big increase in bureaucracy and red tape?" The answer came back overwhelmingly in the affirmative. That is a pretty shocking revelation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and other government apologists who say that the Canadian people are not prepared for some drastic action. I wonder where they get their information.
Cost of Living
I suppose it really should be expected that the head of this commission would be obliged or would feel it necessary to talk in this vein. It must be a very frustrating experience to be named head of an expensive but toothless monster. All the brave words about the effect of the glare of publicity on prices is just nonsense, and the government knows it. It was interesting to read the speech of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray). It is a paraphrasing of, or as a matter of fact it is almost exactly like one which Mackenzie King made in the 1920s. It is really contemporary! Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, it is right up to date-it is not more than 40 years old, about the same age as the minister.
Today, all the Minister of Finance could do in response to a very intelligent speech in this House by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) was to launch a personal attack on the hon. member.
Shame.

The hon. member admits quite candidly that over a period of time he has changed his mind on the basis of new information and changed circumstances. This is a mark of intelligence. But who is the Minister of Finance to cast stones at anyone for changing his mind? No one takes a back seat to the Minister of Finance for mind changing.
Turn-around-Turner.
He has done it a number of times already, several times in this parliament, and no doubt he will do it again. He should certainly change his mind in respect of the incomes policy.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He changed his constituency, too.
Hear, hear!

Being the apologist for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in this case will not save him. If the Liberal Party should ever achieve another majority under its present leadership-heaven [DOT] forbid-the Minister of Finance will not last 18 months, and he knows it. He will be the sacrificial lamb. The Prime Minister will be moved to tears as he is deeply affected at the sight of a man giving his political life for a friend.
Hear, hear!

The government has allowed a desperate situation to develop. The value of the Canadian dollar is declining rapidly. The government blames inflation on external forces. It is a worldwide phenomenon, we are told; the world price of copper is rising; the world price of coffee is rising.
The weather is bad, too.
The North American price of beef is rising; the North American price of lumber is rising; the world price of French wine is rising.

What about the price of fish?

Cost of Living

All of this is quite true. There is an increasing demand and the solution in these cases, of course, is increased production. But all of the coffee, all of the beef, all of the copper and nickel, and indeed the imported wine, is still only a small part of our total inflation in Canada. The major factors are still, first of all, the high cost of government and, second, the cost-push inflation caused by the wage-price spiral.
Tell us about the Bonaventure.

Even the cost of commodities has been influenced greatly by the higher cost of machinery, the higher cost of power, the higher cost of transportation. All of these are factors in the increased cost of commodities. Commodity prices are influenced by higher taxes, as are other prices. As a matter of fact, big government and rising taxes are a major factor in the inflationary cycle.
Hear, hear!

Governments are taking a bigger proportion of the gross national product every year. For the last ten years, each year governments collectively have taken 1 per cent more of the gross national product of Canada than they did the year before. This in itself sets up pressures. It sets up demands for increased wages and it is a directly contributing factor not only to demands for higher wages but also to the increase in prices which in itself results in a demand for higher wages.
In addition to this, the bureaucracy is growing. Just today it was announced that last year the federal bureaucracy in this country grew by 7.3 per cent, and tonight, just a few hours later, the head of the Public Service Commission went on television to apologize for the government. Increasingly, public servants and heads of commissions appointed by this government become little more than apologists for the failures of the government.
Hear, hear!

They do not need to apologize for the government, surely, with all the very talkative members on the opposite side who can defend their own inadequacies without help from public servants. Bureaucracy does not need to grow. The growth is due to new programs that in many cases are of questionable value. It is due to programs which in many cases do not give the taxpayers a fair and adequate return for the tax dollar collected. It is due in many cases to programs which are band-aid treatments, and it is due in large part to the fact that these band-aid programs are a symptom of inadequate and incompetent government in this country. It is a question of treating the symptoms, not the disease.
Then there is the wage-price spiral. Just this week a strike was called because workers refused a 20.5 per cent increase in wages over a two-year contract.
Where?
In the province of Ontario.
Oh, oh!

This was highly inflationary. When a settlement is reached, higher prices will result. It is the old chicken-and-egg situation. Cost-push inflation is still a major component. Higher taxes result in demands for higher wages, which result in higher prices, which result in a squirrel cage situation.
Here is the minister.
I was just going to say that it was a desparate situation. I think it is even more desperate now that the Minister of Finance has joined us.
I hear he is secretly starting to smoke a pipe.

I would not be surprised; I am told it is just as good as transcendental meditation. Prices are rising, and the grocery money is shrinking. Just last Saturday I was talking to a constituent who after she had paid her rent did not have enough money to buy groceries. This is real poverty in its ugliest form. Here is the case of a woman who admits to malnutrition because there is not enough money in her pocket to allow her to buy the groceries necessary for the weekend-and this in a rich country like Canada.
What about housing prices? They are getting out of control to a greater extent every week, every month. The average Canadian citizen cannot afford a decent house for his family. What is the greatest increment of cost in housing? It is the cost of money; it is high interest rates. What do high interest rates do? They bring inflation. And what can be done about it? Nothing, until the Minister of Finance gets off his backside and acts.
Hear, hear!

Just this afternoon in the committee on finance we were told that it costs 10 per cent a year just to hold land until it can be developed. That 10 per cent a year does not include any profit for the owner of the land, merely the cost; and that total cost is due to two increments only, municipal taxes and the cost of money. In response to the direct question we were told that the greatest single cost of maintaining land and holding it to develop, when governments allowed it to be developed, was the cost of money. And the cost of money, we know, is exorbitant due to the lack of action on the part of the government.
We will never solve the housing problem in Canada until inflation is controlled. In the meantime, the government's solution is merely to build more public housing, much of it very necessary but in some cases becoming instant slums. We will never have adequate housing for the people who really need it until inflation is brought under control.
The government wants to increase Canadian participation in the industrial development of the country. It wants to have Canadians play a greater part in our industrial development and resource development. Mr. Speaker, if the government does want Canadians to play a greater part, it will have to make it attractive for Canadians to
June 14, 1973

invest. It will have to restore confidence. It will have to control inflation.
At the present time, people who put their money in the bank have less left in real purchasing power at the end of the year than at the beginning of the year. People who buy savings certificates will be worse off at the end of the year than they were at the beginning of the year. People who buy Canada Savings Bonds will be worse off at the end of the year than they were at the beginning of the year. People who buy Government of Canada Bonds will be worse off at the end of the year than they were at the beginning of the year. People who buy Bell Telephone stock will be worse off at the end of the year than they were at the beginning of the year. As a matter of fact, it is difficult to find an investment in Canada at the present time where you can wind up the year with as much as you had when you started on January 1. So, to attack all the major problems facing Canada today it is necessary to implement radical solutions. New methods must be tried.
The United States is more innovative than Canada. The President of the United States is more radical than the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau).
In more ways than one, that's for sure.

We have to break inflationary expectations. We have to control monopoly power effectively. We have to establish a relationship between wages, prices and productivity in those sectors where price competition does not exist. The objections, and I do not have time to deal with them, are all fallacies. You do not need a big bureaucracy. You do not need to set individual wages and prices. The plans that were tried in Europe are not the kind of policies being put forward over here. All that is necessary is mandatory guidelines, which are like speed limits. If these are put into effect we can bring inflation under control, increase employment and have stable prices. The United States should not have abandoned its stage II. I am sure there is great regret there that they did, and they will have to move back in that direction.
So far as PC policy is concerned, it is contemporary and forward-looking. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has shown the way. The Leader of the Opposition has grasped the nettle. The Leader of the Opposition, in doing so, has become the only contemporary leader of a party in this House of Commons.
Hear, hear!
He is tired of talk. He is tired of excuses. The Leader of the Opposition demands action. Tonight all those members of the House of Commons who really put people's needs-

speechtext: The point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is well taken. The Chair is only seeking some kind of agreement whereby as many members as possible can speak, but I will at this time recognize the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).

Mr. Speaker, President Nixon's proposals for a price freeze yesterday were his fourth attempt to deal with the problem of inflation in the United States. Of phases I, II and III, only phase II was at all successful, and it was successful only temporarily. As soon as the tough controls of phase II were removed and the United States moved to the voluntary controls of phase III, the rate of price increases in the United States jumped to a rate which is even higher than the rate of inflation in Canada at the present time.
Today we have been told by Conservative speakers that they are calling for the imposition in Canada of the kind of program which President Nixon has introduced in the United States. Mr. Speaker, the President's first three phases have been a failure, and the fourth phase announced yesterday has nothing to do with an incomes policy, nothing to do with wage and price controls. His proposals yesterday, aside from the effect of Watergate on President Nixon, were simply a call for price controls. As a matter of fact, President Nixon made it crystal clear yesterday-

Talk about Canada.

June 14, 1973
Cost of Living

I will get to Canada and the Conservative party in a moment. President Nixon made it crystal clear that he was not imposing wage controls because the wage increases achieved by working people in the United States were not inflationary.
The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) who moved this motion today and who, as already has been pointed out, changed his position diametrically from what it was less than two years ago, has called for a temporary freeze on all incomes, to be followed by the working out of an incomes policy. In the few minutes at my disposal I want to look at the proposals which he made on behalf of the Conservative Party.
It is relatively easy to control or freeze wages. It is easy to know precisely what the steelworker in Hamilton, the autoworker in Windsor or Oshawa, and the railway worker in Montreal make per hour and to say that they will not be allowed to make more than 2 per cent, 3 per cent or 5 per cent above that amount in the next year. But I challenge the Conservative Party to say in detail-they have not done it today or any other day-how they would regulate and control the rest of the economy.
Let us look at the things you would have to control if you really are talking about an incomes policy and an equitable distribution of restraint on all sectors of the economy. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) talked about the wage-price spiral. I am not going to say that wages do not have an effect on prices, and the hon. member for Trinity was extremely careful not to say a word about increased profits. So, Mr. Speaker, because hon. members know that I am somewhat biased, let us just turn to the record as it appears in recent issues of the Globe and Mail in the financial pages.
On June 9, 1973, the Globe and Mail carried a story which reported that for the first quarter of 1973, corporation profits were up 53 per cent over the same three months in 1972. That is the biggest quarterly advance in 12 years. On May 1, 1973, the Globe and Mail reported that Canada Packers' profits were up from $10 million the year before to $14 million for the same period this year. On April 19, the Globe and Mail reported that for the first quarter of 1973, International Nickel's profit had risen to $36 million from $1814 million in the same period in 1972, an increase of almost 100 per cent. On May 1, the Globe and Mail reported that Ford Motor Company had a record first quarter profit of $37.6 million, compared to $23.2 million in the first quarter of 1972. On April 27-I pass this along to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander)-the Globe and Mail reported that Dofasco profits had increased to $11,800,000 for the first quarter of 1973, from $8,200,000 for the first quarter of 1972.
And non-union at that.

Dofasco has always claimed that they pay as good or better wages than the organized plants. If that is not true, then I leave it to the hon. member for Hamilton West to explain. If the Conservative Party are serious about an incomes policy, and if they are serious about saying that the wages of workers and salaried people have to be controlled, then what they ought to tell the business

community is that their income tax policy-if and when they form the government-will be to amend the Income Tax Act to provide for a 100 per cent excess profits tax on all profits higher than the base period which they will establish. Of course, they would not dare do that.
They don't say "Hear, hear" to that.
We include profits in the plan, though.

The hon. member for Saint-Hyaeinthe (Mr. Wagner) said that prices should be frozen except for unprocessed food at the farm gate. I find that a very interesting proposal. I wonder which member of parliament is prepared to tell the farmers of this country that if Canada Packers, Kraft, Dominion Stores or Safeway cannot raise their price to the consumer, they are going to pay one penny more than they are paying to the farmers for the unprocessed foodstuff they produce. It is nonsense to say that if you control prices at the retail level you will not have to control prices to the farmers. I think the farmers know this, and the members of the Conservative Party ought to keep that in mind.
What about the professional person? How would a Conservative government put controls on the incomes of selfemployed people? There has been a Conservative government in the province of Ontario for 30 years, and they still have not found a way to put any kind of limit on the incomes of doctors in Ontario which are increasing by leaps and bounds every year. I suggest that the federal Conservative Party would be no more successful than the Conservative Party in Ontario.
In the newspaper which has the largest circulation in Canada there appeared today an interesting article by Anthony Westell in which he called for an incomes control policy and said, in effect, "Do as I say, not as I do". Mr. Westell used to be chief correspondent for the Toronto Star in Ottawa, but he left that job and is now a professor at Carleton University. I assume that is where most of his income comes from, but in his spare time he moonlights and writes the odd article for the Toronto Star.
"Odd" is right.

If Mr. Westell wants to write three articles a week in the Toronto Star instead of just one or two, his income will go up; but of course it is easy for him to recommend that the ordinary worker in Canada Packers, Dofasco or some other plant should have his income controlled. Mr. Westell knows that as he is self-employed he does not have to worry about that.
I want to return to the question of food prices, Mr. Speaker. My wife is just as concerned about the cost of food as is any wife in Canada. I wonder how freezing the price of foodstuffs will affect the tremendous percentage of that cost which goes for fruits and vegetables which are imported for six months of the year or more from other parts of the world. We import oranges from the United States, Mexico, Israel and Spain; we import lettuce from the United States and Mexico; we import pineapples and grapefruit-in fact we import all foodstuffs except meats. Prices are going up every week. Does the Conservative Party expect that we can freeze those prices? They do not
June 14, 1973

have the answer, Mr. Speaker; and they have not tried to answer, because there is no answer. They propose that we fix prices. Well, a large percentage of Canada's major products are exported, such as, paper, copper, zinc, nickel, wheat-
Lumber.
We export lumber-
And the cost of houses is going up.

I have not heard one member of the Conservative Party suggest a two-price system for the products which we export. Without a two-price system, what we would be doing if we fixed the price at the present rate, and the world price for those commodities went up, would be subsidizing consumers in the United States, Japan and other countries which buy our products.
I think I have indicated very clearly, Mr. Speaker, that even if an incomes policy makes sense, even if it is possible-and I question that very much-it is certainly not possible on the basis of the proposals or suggestions detailed by the Conservative Party today or any other day, in parliament or outside. Having said that, I want to make it clear that I do not accept the present government's policy of doing nothing about the increased cost of living.
What can be done? Where are the major increases in the cost of living taking place? First of all, they are taking place in the cost of housing. I suggest that a great deal could be done about this. The Government of Canada could tell the chartered banks and insurance companies of Canada that they must allocate a substantial percentage of the money they have available for lending to the field of residential housing in order to meet the needs of many for residential accommodation, and that they should lend the money at prime rates of interest.
If the people could obtain money for houses at 7 per cent or T1/ per cent instead of, as at present, 914 per cent or 10 per cent, which will be the rate in the not too distant future, the people of Canada would save substantial amounts of money. I have calculated roughly that on a $20,000 mortgage, if instead of paying 10 per cent, which will be the going rate at the end of the year, a person could pay 7 per cent he would save $600 per year or $50 a month. That amount would really be significant in meeting the increase in the cost of living.
As well, I suggest that the federal government co-operate with the provinces in establishing a land bank assembly program. Let us get rid of the developers who are fattening themselves and speculating with land at the expense of the housing consumer.
What will you do with them, shoot them?
What about food prices?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have much time left. I only want to say that the solution of the Progressive Conservative Party to check the increase in the cost of living and price increases is to freeze incomes.
In other words, the income of those who are defenseless, namely the majority of producers, farmers, fishermen, will be frozen across the board. The man who, in my riding, works in a fish factory for $1.60 or $1.75 an hour, will have its salary frozen. That is the solution proposed by the Progesssive Conservative Party in the current situation.
Mr. Speaker, faced with this situation, the government has proposed fair solutions. Indeed, it tries to improve the net income of Canadians by increasing the old age pension, by establishing programs to help the have nots, those who are defenseless. In other words, instead of acting negatively and freezing incomes, high or low, we are saying that we are going to increase the net income of Canadians.
Some members of the Progressive Conservative Party are trying to talk of the components of misery. Yet, I must remind them that under the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal government shares 50 per cent of the cost of this plan.
